subtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCREASE DEDUCTION IN RESPECT OF PROVINCIAL TAX

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROPOSAL TO INCREASE DEDUCTION IN RESPECT OF PROVINCIAL TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement about the developments resulting from the imposition of a provincial income tax in the province of Quebec.
As all hon. members are aware, I had a meeting with the premier of Quebec, at his request, on October 5 last in Montreal. Mr. Duplessis indicated, at that time, that he was considering proposing certain amendments to the provincial income tax law which he hoped might make possible some temporary agreement which would give both governments a further opportunity to arrive at more satisfactory permanent arrangements. He undertook, at that time, to write to me indicating the nature of the changes it was proposed to make in the provincial income tax and to suggest a basis for a temporary agreement.
In a letter dated November 1, he indicated the changes he was prepared to make in order to reach an agreement for the deduction of the provincial tax from the federal tax.
Since the receipt of his letter, my colleagues and I have been giving the most careful consideration to the problem and during the course of that consideration it was arranged by the two governments that some of our officials would visit Quebec to secure certain factual information without which it was not possible to have a complete picture of what, I am sure all hon. members will agree, are some of the most difficult and complex problems we face in the practical working of our Canadian confederation, namely, the appropriate fiscal relationships between the federal and provincial governments.
The problem of finding any basis for a temporary agreement was complicated by the fact that the Quebec income tax act provided different exemptions and a different apportionment from the federal Income Tax Act. The more we studied the problem the clearer it became that if, as always has been our policy, the same treatment in respect of federal taxes was to be available to Canadian
taxpayers in whatever province they lived, we could not agree to the deduction from the federal tax of the tax imposed in one province unless in similar circumstances and without too seriously affecting federal revenues we could agree to the deduction of a similar tax imposed in any other province.
Mr. Duplessis had, however, indicated in his letter that the probable yield from the provincial tax was equal to about 10 per cent of the total of the federal income tax collected in the province of Quebec. This statement led us to consider whether, in some way which could be applied in any province, it would be possible to make room for the collection of a provincial tax which would yield 10 per cent of the federal tax in that province, without the necessity of any taxpayer in the province having to pay a higher tax that he would have to pay on the same income in any other province.
The estimated figures of tax yields in all the provinces for 1954 were carefully scrutinized and it appeared from these figures that it would be possible to reduce the federal tax by 10 per cent in any province which preferred not to have a tax rental agreement, and still safeguard the revenues necessary to meet our irreducible national responsibilities.
The estimates of the yields for 1954 and figures for previous years were carefully examined to see whether a greater reduction, which would have to be available to any province, would be possible. In the light of our responsibilities to the whole Canadian people we reached the conclusion that we could not, at this time, recommend any reduction greater than 10 per cent of the federal tax in a province which did not have a tax rental agreement.
At the present time a taxpayer having to pay a provincial income tax may claim a deduction up to 5 per cent of his federal tax. There are administrative difficulties and complications for taxpayers in deducting a portion of one tax from another, but what is even more serious, this method makes the real incidence of the provincial tax depend on the terms of the federal law and makes the total amount deducted from the federal tax depend on the terms of the provincial law. We feel that it would be more satisfactory to reduce the federal income tax by a fixed percentage in any province which imposes and collects a provincial tax and

Federal-Provincial Fiscal Relations thereby let both federal and provincial taxes stand on their own feet without either government having to provide for a deduction of one tax from the other.
I have, accordingly, advised the premiers of all the provinces that we propose, pending the results of a new federal-provincial conference, to ask parliament to amend the federal income tax law in order to make a reduction of 10 per cent for all taxpayers of any province where a provincial income tax is levied on income for the years 1955 and 1956. At the same time we will ask parliament to release from its present tax rental agreement any province which would prefer the new arrangement.
We also intend to propose that income tax payers who have actually paid a provincial income tax on their 1954 income be allowed a deduction up to 10 per cent of their federal tax. In practice, of course, this higher deduction for 1954 will be applicable only to taxpayers who have paid the Quebec income tax because no other province had a provincial income tax in operation in 1954.
In any case the figures already available make it clear that the rentals for the personal and corporation income tax fields in every province for 1954 will be greater than the amount the provincial governments could have raised from a 7 per cent tax on corporation incomes and a personal income tax equal to 10 per cent of the federal tax.
These proposed amendments are intended only as a stopgap arrangement pending the conclusion of any long term arrangements for the period following the expiry of the present tax rental agreements.
As hon. members know it had always been understood that it would be necessary to hold a federal-provincial conference before the end of 1955 to discuss fiscal arrangements for the years which will follow.
In the light of the recent developments, it may be the desire of the provincial governments to have this conference held at an earlier date. I have addressed letters to the premiers of all the provinces outlining the proposal I have just mentioned and inviting the nine provinces which have tax rental agreements to indicate whether they would prefer to take advantage of the proposed new arrangement. In these letters I have indicated that shortly after my return from the commonwealth prime ministers' meeting in London I shall communicate with them further with the view to working out arrangements for a conference at a time which will be satisfactory to all governments concerned.
I should like now to table the letters I have exchanged with the premier of Quebec and the letter I addressed to the premiers of the other nine provinces.

The proposed economic survey of the Passamaquoddy bay tidal power project is, of course, not a new proposal. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Would he consider

setting aside a day for the purpose of discussing some of the matters that might be presented before the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London so as to enable hon. members to know in general what views the Prime Minister will express on behalf of the Dominion of Canada? I would also ask whether he will place before the house the agenda of that conference which apparently has been referred to in London and is not concealed there. I am sure hon. members would wish to know what views the Prime Minister intends to present on behalf of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR DISCUSSION OF AGENDA FOR CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I could say to the house what views I will be expressing in the course of the discussions that may take place in London, but I would, of course, be glad to hear views expressed in the house as to what would be the appropriate attitude to take there.
The conference has been called for the discussion of both political and economic problems, and I know there have been some indications of the general line the agenda is apt to follow. However, the agenda is usually settled at the opening meeting of the conference because it has always been the practice to recognize that those attending are, at least as far as status is concerned, of equal rank and that each would have the same right to indicate what he felt it would be proper to have the conference deal with. I think it would be advisable to see just what further course this debate on the address takes. It is understood that on Thursday, January 20, there will be an interruption of the debate, if not concluded by that time, in order to deal with external affairs, and we will see then what can be done to meet the suggestion made by the hon. member.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DISCUSSION OF AGENDA FOR CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS

We would like to know what attitude the Prime Minister will take on a matter such as this.

speechtext:
I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the withdrawal of financial support for civil defence by the Montreal city council and somewhat similar action by Victoria, British Columbia, about three months ago, has the minister any plans to prevent the disappearance of civil defence measures in those populous areas and the strong possibility of the same sort of thing happening in other cities following their example?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED WITHDRAWAL OF FINANCIAL SUPPORT BY MONTREAL AND VICTORIA, B.C., CITY COUNCILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman did not give me any notice of his question, but I am able to deal with it. In the first place I may say to him that the city


council of Montreal has not made a decision to vacate the civil defence field. The executive committee of the governing body of the city of Montreal has made a recommendation to that effect, to become effective on May 1. As soon as I heard of this particular intention I had the civil defence co-ordinator, after consultation with the provincial authorities who are interested in the matter of civil defence, enter into negotiations with officials of the executive body to which I have made reference. Those negotiations are going on and, as a result of representations that are being made to that body indicating in particular that now for the first time funds are available from the federal government directly to the municipalities concerned, I have every hope that the governing body in that particular community will want to reverse its position. In any event, the decision is one that does not rest alone with that body but with the whole metropolitan area in the city of Montreal.
It is true that the city of Victoria made a similar decision but I am happy to say that, as a result of the negotiations carried on by the civil defence co-ordinator and the municipal government in Victoria, the latter reversed its position. Mr. Speaker I have been listening with attention and a great deal of interest to the important statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has just made to the house with regard to fiscal relations between the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec. At this stage I have no comment to offer. I do reserve the right, however, to draw my own conclusions in due course.
When I had the advantage and privilege of rising in this house for the first time, in November 1953, I stated, as will be found in Hansard:
It is all good and well to praise and appreciate the highly social legislation on family allowances, which was adopted by the parliament of Canada, some years ago. It has contributed substantially in raising the standard of living of our large families, even if today, due to the constant rise in the cost of living and to overtaxation, it no longer achieves its original purpose.
Today, more than ever, family allowances are insufficient, since they represent hardly half the value they had when they were first initiated. I am not speaking for any political group in particular, but I defer willingly to the wishes and to the repeated requests of all the large families of my constituency, to whom I have promised my support. I therefore, on their behalf, request the government to raise these allowances appreciably in order to give these families the advantage of greater purchasing power, which is the only guarantee of economic prosperity. Up to what level should these allowances be raised? Here is a question, it seems to me, to which the answer is easily found.
If parliament, last year, deemed it advisable to double parliamentary indemnities, the government being of the opinion that the expenses of members had increased in that same proportion, I consider that such is the case with Canadian families, which must, the same as we, buy the necessities of life. I can anticipate the following question: Where can we get the money to bring a greater measure of welfare into our homes? Here again the answer is very simple. We can get the money from the savings that can be made in the different departments of the government and especially the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production.
We want to ward off and curb unemployment. The means to that end do not seem very complicated to me. Let us start by reducing personal income taxes, thus putting

more buying power in the hands of the Canadian people. Let us reduce corporation taxes, and we shall have greater investments for the development of our great resources. On that score I endorse this statement of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce:
Taxes should never become excessive to the point of taking away from industry the stimulus of a reasonable profit and from the individual the possibility of saving some money. In a growing country over-taxation affects the system which makes possible our development and our progress in the field of social welfare. Any trend towards a reduction of profits through taxation is a trend towards instability in the field of business. Every enterprise should be allowed to keep enough of its profits to enable it to develop on a solid basis in an expanding economy and to face the hazards of competition.

All members of the house will certainly agree, Mr. Speaker, that so far I have never been afraid to express my convictions, not only political but religious and patriotic as well. Personally I have great admiration for those who are not afraid to state in the house what they are and what they think. I have no hesitation at all in replying to the fiery and bitter statements directed against my province in this house by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). In order to be understood by him and that small number who may share his opinions, I will speak in his own language. Will the member permit me to inform him that by his foolish speech he has earned for himself the unenviable honour of being the most narrow-minded Canadian I have ever met. The hon. member was not afraid to demonstrate his gift for fanaticism. In doing so he has endeavoured, in a few minutes, to do more to raise the race cry and to disunite the country than has been accomplished since confederation.

That is the first time the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis) has agreed with the hon. member for Quebec West. In the few minutes he has spent in Quebec, which no doubt he was visiting for the first time, to his great astonishment he found that we were not like others; that our language and our faith were not that of the majority. Furthermore, he found out that our educational system was different from that of the other provinces. In other words he found that we rightly retained rights and characteristics which will not be given up, no matter how much the party to which he belongs would like to see them disappear. As his leader has not denounced these words, we take for granted that our way of life in Quebec, our liberties, our habits and our

attributes have always been and will always be an obstacle to the success of that party in our province.
The hon. member has spoken of Quebec as another nation. He has classified the valiant and distinguished premier as the master of this other nation. If by that term he intended to insult one who will go down in history as having been the greatest premier that province has ever known, and for whom we in Quebec have great admiration and respect, may I say, Mr. Speaker, that that sort of insult will never achieve what he has in mind. No doubt the hon. member forgets his history, and it may be well to remind him of it. The French-speaking Canadians are no strangers to Canadian soil. It was our ancestors who were the first pioneers in this land; they were also the first to contribute to make Canada what it is today. The contribution the people of our province have made to the development of Canada is an immense one, and more than once our English-speaking compatriots have paid tribute to this contribution.
We have generously put to the service of Canada our French culture. Does the hon. member reproach us for keeping intact our language, our faith, our habits and our attachment to our institutions, and to those who see to it that these things are maintained? We shall not abandon our prerogatives, first because we are faithfully and religiously attached to them, and secondly because the fathers of confederation, who possessed a much broader mind than that of the hon. member, have guaranteed those prerogatives to us by a contract. It is not merely a sheet of paper, and it is called the British North America Act. May God preserve us from ever having a socialist government. Under a socialist regime, with policies such as the hon. member advocates, we would see the end of our constitutional liberty. It would mean anarchy and disunity. In one word, we would be powerlessly watching the funeral of our democratic rights.
He said that for many years the people of Quebec did not get the old age pension benefits enjoyed by other provinces. We had to get rid of the Liberal government in our province, Mr. Speaker, in order that that social measure would be applied. We did get those benefits on the day the present premier took power in our province. How many battles did he conduct from his seat in the opposition on this very subject? Never in all its history has the province of Quebec known such expansion in its economy. Never have our immense resources been so generously used for the benefit of our people. Our

The hon. member need not worry. With the strength of our religious convictions, with the honour and respect we have for our clergy to whom we owe in great measure our survival as an ethnic group, and bearing in mind the glorious past of our ancestors, with the love we have for democracy, we are as solid as the fortifications of Quebec against that evil ideology. Even if the rest of the country ever fell into the hands of the masters of the Kremlin, which is absurd to contemplate, Canada would still have a bastion that would guard and keep the standard of liberty and democracy-Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to speak at this time. I came to the second session of the twenty-second parliament with a good deal of concern about the economic conditions in Canada, and indeed the financial position and economic conditions of many of our people. I am sorry that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is not in his seat. I see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is still in the house, and in the course of my remarks I shall make some reference to what he said with respect to the agricultural picture in Canada.
I first wish to say that my concern is over the fact that in this rich country of Canada we have upwards of half a million people unemployed. I do not think it is possible properly to assess the total number of people who are unemployed, but I am quite certain that hon. members will agree that there are well over half a million. When one considers that, and also the number of dependents who must look to the breadwinner for sustenance, then he can understand the serious plight of hundreds of thousands of our people in this rich country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who made it rich?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I realize that when we come back and hear government spokesmen, such as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture, we hear the same old story that we have heard from

1945 to the present time. Many of the conditions that existed then are still plaguing the Canadian economy. We have unemployment; we have farm people who are losing their equity in their farms. We have foreclosures and all the other things which do bring hardships to many of our people.
When I hear the expression "You have never had it better" I try to find out where the ministers and others from the government side of the house get such assurance that everything is all right. I come from an agricultural area where we have had the worst crop failure in the last ten years. One cannot but be concerned; but when he turns to some other parts of our economy he gets the reassurance that some people in Canada are in a very good financial position.
I went to the library and brought back the "Financial Post Survey of Industrials" in Canada for the year 1954. I quite agree with hon. members on the government side of the house and those who take a philosophical attitude toward conditions in Canada at the present time, I agree, indeed, that many of the bigger corporations are in a healthy financial position. I shall read a short paragraph indicating that some of these companies have a buoyant income. This survey states:
Based on an analysis by the Financial Post of the latest published annual reports, the combined net profit of 32S companies in 1953 was 3 per cent ahead of the 1952 level. Earnings before depreciation, interest and taxes were 2 per cent below the previous year.
The report goes on to say:
Percentage return on combined net assets continued in its downward trend of recent years,-
But this is the point; the profit return amounted to 10-04 per cent. So far as these 326 industrials in Canada are concerned, they are still in a buoyant financial position and are receiving very good returns. However, the picture is not so happy when one turns to the farming people of Canada. Before I go into that I wish to say that, according to the speech from the throne, we can look for a little alleviation of the hardships of some of our people. I welcome the fact that there is to be an increase in the war veterans allowance; but I say here and now that it is long overdue. The move should have been made long before this. The cost of living has gone up steadily since 1945, and nothing has been done to help these war veterans. When the government bring in the measure, I hope they will accept the suggestion of the Legion, who are asking that the allowance be raised to $60 for single veterans and $120 for married couples.
In addition, I welcome the disability pension that the government has seen fit
The Address-Mr. E. G. McCullough to enact. On looking over the proposals, it occurred to me that they are too rigid and too strict. There are far too many people who cannot earn a living and who are dependent upon others who will not be able to qualify. I hope the government will see fit to make the regulations less stringent. Also the government has brought in a meagre program of public works suggesting that Ripple Rock be removed and a few other public works projects. I want to say here and now I do not think that will meet the great need we have in Canada for a real public works program by which we can put our unemployed back to work. As I recall, last February the unemployment insurance benefits paid out of the public treasury to the unemployed was in excess of $28 million and so I say that in this rich country we should have a program which will meet the developments and the needs of our people.
Now I wish to discuss the farm picture and to discredit, I think, the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and in this regard I want first to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Estevan, Saskatchewan, Mercury dated December 23, 1954. This paper is published in my own constituency and in respect to the farm income for the coming year it says, and I quote:
The growing threat of a world-wide economic recession has been removed by an upsurge in business conditions in most countries that are Canada's customers for wheat.
Before continuing I want to say that the editor must be misinformed because, as everyone knows, the reason there is a demand for Canadian wheat in these countries where we normally market our wheat is the fact that those countries have suffered crop failures this past year. More particularly I want to stress this, and again I quote:
In this regard the poor wheat crop in Canada has been a blessing in disguise.
As far as I am concerned that is nothing short of capitalist mental neurosis. I think that when we have in this country people who can produce for a hungry world and we have an editorial which says that the crop failure which we have suffered this year in western Canada is a blessing in disguise there is something wrong with the thinking of those people. I think it can be attributed to the capitalist psychology all the way down the line because the capitalist society has never been able to take care of abundance at any time. Perhaps hon. members on the other side of the house and the right hon. Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will perhaps now be chuckling deep down in their

The Address

Mr. E. G. McCullough collars that once again nature has pulled us out of a task which cannot be accomplished in a capitalist set-up, such as we have today, in spite of the fact that we on this side of the house have pleaded with the government to undertake a program for agriculture under which when through the bounty of Providence we have in this country an abundance of wheat, we can store it for the lean years.
I need not repeat what I said in the past that this was done in Egypt over two thousand years ago. In the years of plenty they stored for the years of scarcity. There is no one single thing which could injure the western hemisphere more than a continued crop failure which could put the balance of negotiations and what have you on the side of the iron curtain. Yet in this country, where we have steel and concrete and where we could store our wheat for the years of scarcity which might come, there is no program. The only way that the government has got out from under it is by a widespread crop failure in western Canada.
What is the situation in respect to farm income in western Canada? Quite briefly we have had the most serious decline in the last twenty years. According to dominion bureau of statistics figures net farm income was as follows:
1951	$2,188,600,000
1952	 1,949,900,000
1953		 1,667,000,000
1954	(estimate)	 1,200,000,000
This represents a three-year decline of one-half of the 1951 net farm income. In Saskatchewan, the province whence I come, we will have a net income this year of $250 million less than in 1953, or a drop of approximately 46 per cent.
I want to carry the same argument through to show the condition of agriculture in Canada. Taking the period from 1935 to 1939 as the base period, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, from July 1951 to October 1953, manufactured goods in Canada declined 15-6 points. But farm products, that is, the wholesale price index of farm products, dropped 68-6, a difference of 53 points. There is a decline to 1954 and today western farmers are finding themselves in a definite price squeeze. Their costs are up and their income is going down.
What does this mean to the purchasing power of the farmer? According to the dominion bureau of statistics report again, we have the index of commodities and services used by farmers, taking again the base
[Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain) .1

period from 1935 to 1939, standing at 225- these are the things which are used by farmers in the production of the various farm commodities-an increase of 125 points since 1939.
What does this mean to the farmer in relation to the money with which he can purchase these commodities? As an example let us consider wheat. No. 1 is now $1.72 f.o.b. Fort William, and in terms of 19351939 purchasing power it is worth only 76 cents. That is the problem facing western Canada today and I think this government should take cognizance of that fact. This condition affects the whole economy. I am not here to plead for the farmers of western Canada particularly but for every last citizen who has to earn his bread and butter in Canada and maintain a home and provide for his children.
Concerning retail sales in Canada there was a drop of $214 million in the first nine months of 1954. According to the unemployment figures again there are 18,000 unemployed as of November 1954 in Winnipeg, 20,000 in Vancouver; and in Yorkton, Saskatchewan, a very small city, the registered unemployed figure has increased by 70 per cent from the previous year.
Again I have indicated that some of the companies in Canada are still making hay. I remember the story that was told in this house, I think by the premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Thomas Douglas, when he was indicating that the fun which the big corporations have can perhaps be compared to the elephant who dances around in the chicken house. It is fine fun for the elephant but it is pretty tough on the chickens.
I am saying that the little enterprise, the small businessman, the small enterpriser is being driven to the wall in many cases. According to the dominion bureau of statistics figures commercial failures for the first nine months of 1954 rose to 1,684 from 1,127 in the preceding year.
I would like to turn to the statement made in this house on January 10 by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when, in reply to the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe), he stated, as reported at page 32 of Hansard:
The hon. gentleman has said that Canada has lost the United Kingdom market for the second time in his own period of political experience. There has been no loss of the United Kingdom market.
I think it is quite unnecessary for me to again put on record the figures I gave last year dealing with exports from this country

to the United Kingdom from 1939 to 1953, the latest date for which figures were then available. But I would like to give comparative figures for farming commodities exported to the United Kingdom, and as will be found in the dominion bureau of statistics return dated March 18, 1954. The figures are given in hundredweights. In 1945, of beef and veal Canada shipped 1,843,777 and in 1953 the amount fell to 64,501 cwt. In 1946 we shipped 103,243 cwt. of fresh lamb and mutton and in 1953 not a single pound. In 1943 we shipped 149,124 cwt. of fresh pork and in 1953 no shipments at all. In 1947 we shipped 120,988 cwt. of poultry and in 1953 again nothing. In 1944 we shipped 6,923,103 cwt. of bacon and hams to Britain and in 1953 nothing. In canned meats we shipped 338,378 cwt. in 1944 and in 1953 only 27. We shipped 142,300 cwt. of edible offal in 1944 and in 1953 not a single pound. As regards "other meats", we shipped 1,995 cwt. in 1946 and 10 cwt. in 1953.

would like to draw the minister's attention to something he said the other day, on his return from the United States, with respect to the support prices we have on some Canadian commodities. The minister seems quite satisfied with these support prices, particularly with reference to the poultry producers in this country. They feel they are not getting a fair deal, and that the support price is too high in relation to what they get. I had a conversation recently with a local storekeeper who takes eggs from the farms and ships them to the packing houses, and two years ago they were paying around 21 cents a dozen for mixed eggs. I asked the dealer how he came out, and where the principle of support price entered into the transaction. He showed me a return on 24 dozen crates of eggs and it proved that he had lost $4 on that quantity. I asked him whether he got any return from the packers, and he said, "No, that is all I get." What in effect was happening was that they were handling them as a service.
In this regard I would point out that despite that situation the minister indicated the other day that in Canada the support price for eggs and for poultry was working out satisfactorily.

speechtext:
I do
not wish to encroach upon the time of other hon. members, and in the few minutes at my disposal I want to make five suggestions which might help us to combat the economic difficulties now facing the nation.
I believe the greatest challenge to the western democracies is that of putting their own house in order and providing the people with security and a decent standard of living. With regard to unemployment the federal government in 1945 committed itself to complete responsibility for all unemployed employables in Canada in lieu of the provinces giving up certain taxation rights. I want to say to the government that it is high time they took that responsibility and, if necessary, called another reconstruction conference and get down to business with the provinces. I do not think there is one single province that would hesitate to meet with the government. If it undertook its responsibility in respect of the unemployed in Canada, I think the provinces would do their part. I know my own province of Saskatchewan is quite ready to take on responsibility for the disabled and those who are unemployable. That is one thing. Coupled with that matter, we should have some vision in the matter of a public works project across Canada, worked out with the provinces and the municipalities, whereby we may have social projects which will benefit them and which will put our people to work on a work and wages basis.
As I say-and I referred to this matter in the earlier part of my speech-this government should look after those who are war veterans under the war veterans allowance and immediately increase that allowance as requested by the Legion up to $60 for a single person or $120 for married couples. This government should undertake immediately what this party has always asked, namely a health insurance program for every citizen in Canada. It is something which the government is going to have to give some thought to. Unless action is taken quickly, you will have to find new ground and new data which will make it possible that, when you make


up your mind-if and when you do so-you can undertake it with some success and assure that it will have the necessary personnel, the necessary hospitals and other things in order to put it into operation. I urge the government to bring in a national health program for the people. It is long overdue. We need it right now. This government should undertake now to start training girls in the nursing profession. They could undertake to help the provinces. Up to this time they have not done so. I realize that assistance is given for the construction of hospitals, but this government should take a real lead in having each of the provinces bring their hospitals up to the maximum necessary to give adequate hospitalization under a national hospitalization scheme because there will be many more people who will then have an opportunity to go to hospital but who now, through the hit or miss program of personal hospitalization, are not able to get the health care they need.
In conclusion I want to deal with the farm program. As I said before, this is not a selfish approach because I come from a predominantly agricultural province but rather because I think it would be for the welfare of all of Canada. First of all I think this government should do something seriously about its trade policies. I think the government should get these trade envoys, the people who are out trying to sell Canadian products, to get off their soft chairs and get out and do something about this matter so that Canadian markets will be extended so that we shall have a marked step in the direction of freer trade.
Then in respect of our domestically consumed farm products, may I say that I think the government should establish a national livestock marketing board; and under that board they should set prices for agricultural commodities-that is livestock products and dairy products-which will give the cost of production. In that formula there should be forward pricing by which the producer would know, for two or three years, the minimum amount he is going to get for his products. To date the Agricultural Prices Support Act has been used in some cases to support agricultural products, but to date only in the neighbourhood of $80 million has been used under this fund. The minister shakes his head. He can perhaps give the house other figures. That is my figure and I went and looked it up. The figure I have is $80 million whereas, on the other hand, we find that $60 million has been paid in subsidies to the gold mining industry. I am not trying to make an issue of that or any comparison; but surely the agricultural welfare of this

country is worth more than $80 million. I therefore say that through a national livestock marketing board we should have this guaranteed price which will give the cost of production to our farm people and tend to give equilibrium to all our economy because, as I have said before, when the farm economy is in the doldrums then you have your dependent industries such as the farm machinery industry and the others in a depressed condition.
Then again I have spoken about dairy products. They too should be under the same system of forward pricing, with guaranteed prices over a period of years. Another thing which could be done is the institution of a crop insurance program. Speaking the other day the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) outlined something in that regard. I am not going to go into it other than to say this. Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act there is not sufficient coverage and guarantee that the farmer who loses his crop, through drought, hail or flooding, can receive a proper income or any assistance under that act. There is therefore a great need there. In asking this I do not think that I am being unreasonable. Protection is given to every other industry in Canada. We are just asking that, for the sake of the welfare of the whole economy, something substantial be done in order to prevent the fluctuations which we find in the agricultural picture.
In conclusion I just want to say this. Unless this government is ready to come out of its hiding and do something for the Canadian people I think-and quite justly so-that there will be an aroused public and that the people of this country who are without jobs and the farmers who are losing their equity in their land and are having their farm machinery repossessed, are going to rise up in wrath which is quite justifiable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few minutes in this debate. First, I should like you to know that I agree most heartily with the congratulations that have been extended to the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Car-rick) for their splendid contributions to this debate.
I listened closely to the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) when he set forth the policies of his party. I was hoping to hear some constructive suggestions as to what the government should do and what this once great party would do if they were sitting in the seats of government. I was glad to hear that the Acting Leader of the Opposition has committed his followers to a program of national contributory health
The Address-Mr. McLeod insurance in co-operation with the provinces. I was somewhat amused at the reaction of our socialist friends to this announcement. They have always tried to steal the limelight by laying claim to originating and forcing the government to take action in connection with all the matters of social welfare legislation that have been put on the statute books.
I think it would be well for us all to bear in mind the fact that the Canadian people are a humanitarian race and like to alleviate suffering and misery wherever it may be found. But I can assure you that they do not like to have it done under state control or under too much regimentation. I also noticed that part of the subamendment to the speech from the throne where the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) inserts the words "have deliberately returned to the policy of uncontrolled and unplanned private enterprise".
We in this corner of the house had begun to fear, as our leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), said the other day, that the Liberals were socialists in low gear. However, we are glad to learn now that they have returned to the fold of free enterprise. I make no apology for claiming that our group since its inception has continuously and unwaveringly supported the system of free enterprise. We have stood by this policy throughout the years and while we admit that limited controls may sometimes be necessary we will oppose any move by this or any other government to place the affairs of the Canadian people under state control or to regiment our way of life.
Since neither the amendment nor the subamendment offers anything concrete, we may as well consider the speech from the throne itself. We are glad to note that the international situation has improved. While the peace in Korea may be an uneasy one, the bloodshed has at least ceased. There is a possibility that affairs in Indo-China may be stabilized and I trust that the Canadian members of the commission that has been given the tremendous task of overseeing the carrying out of plans in that part of the world will, with the other members of the commission, work towards ultimate success, stabilize affairs in that country and bring about lasting peace.
In a few days we shall be debating in the house the London and Paris agreements. I think we should all remember the steadfast leadership of Sir Anthony Eden who is so greatly responsible for bringing these agreements out of what seemed total failure. I know that the problem of the admission of Germany to NATO causes much concern, but we trust

The Address-Mr. McLeod that it will be given very careful consideration in the house and throughout the country and that by our actions we will contribute something towards the removal of this stumbling block to world peace which exists in Europe today. All in all, international conditions are more settled than for some time. World leaders predict an era of peace. I wonder whether we are ready for it. That is a terrible question to ask but I am sincere. Are we ready for peace?
In our lifetime we have noticed that good times and bad times have coincided with war and peace. Under the stimulus and demands of war, either for industry or for the armed services, the energy of every one of our citizens is required, and so we have full employment. The resulting increase in wages and income places in the hands of our people a supply of purchasing power so that they can buy the goods and services required for daily living. Then we have good times. Good times, Mr. Speaker, but under the stress and worry of war we are not able to enjoy them.
After the demands of war are satisfied and we return to a peacetime economy we then find that the demands of industry for labour gradually taper off and we have lessened wages and income with lessened purchasing power in the hands of our people. Then we have bad times. I do not think I need elaborate further. We have all witnessed the cycle, good times and bad times, war and peace, boom and bust. The solution is sustained production, production that will supply the materials for roads, bridges, houses for our people, public buildings for educational and health services, land clearing, natural resources development. I could continue. These must replace wartime production. The program is unlimited but leadership must come from the government and the finances for the program must be supplied by the government on a non-interest bearing basis by the issuance of currency and credit through our own institution, the Bank of Canada.
I am not pessimistic about our economic problems, Mr. Speaker. I have wonderful faith in the resources of our country and in the ability of our people to work and to produce. We are now entering an era of peace and it is the duty of the government to give the necessary leadership to see that we are not entering an era of depression. We are finding it difficult to employ all our workers. We have surpluses of agricultural products. We have our warehouses filled with goods that our people and the peoples of the world need badly. We have idle factories. These are signs we must heed. These things create

problems that we must face instead of sitting back and hoping that something will happen to pull us out of the mess.
I am glad that such prompt action has been taken to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to alleviate the condition of our unemployed, but this is only a stopgap. It is not a cure for unemployment. I note that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will attend a conference of commonwealth prime ministers in London shortly. I trust that he will have constructive ideas to place before the conference for improving trade with these countries. I hope he is successful, for it is very essential that we have increased twoway trade within the commonwealth, especially with Great Britain. I trust that our trade emissaries trying to bolster GATT will meet with ultimate success.
I have heard the more or less humorous criticism of the cabinet that they are commercial travellers. I should like to commend the government for the leadership it is giving in trying to open outlets for our goods in the world markets. I think we are all agreed that in this era of highly competitive trade personal contact is the better way to sell goods. Not only are these travellers selling goods but we hope they are selling Canada. Even if the bill is $60 million it is not too much to pay for good will. A few days ago the phrase "peace and good will" was on everyone's lips. We are spending about $2 billion a year to promote and preserve peace. Surely $60 million is not too high a price for good will.
I should like to devote a few minutes now to local affairs. Last summer I was glad to have the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), who is present in the house, and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) visit my riding. I say "riding", Mr. Speaker. I did not have the privilege of seeing them. I was glad to note that the Minister of Fisheries had set the minds of the people of Vernon at rest with regard to the new federal building in that city. I had advised them earlier that the Department of Public Works would proceed with the building in 1955 and it was nice to have this confirmed on the spot by a cabinet minister.
I should like to assure the Minister of Public Works that the need for more post office space and for centralized government offices is becoming more urgent in Vernon. This year we are suffering a recession in our two great industries, farming and lumbering, and government projects to provide extra jobs and extra purchasing power are badly needed. Some of you do not seem to realize that we have an agricultural industry in British Columbia. I do not blame you, for so many

members of the house would have you believe that agriculture starts at the Manitoba boundary and ends at the British Columbia line.
Despite the fact that we have a good agricultural industry, we have our troubles as well. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) champion the cause of New Brunswick farmers a few days ago. I was pleased also to hear him take the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) to task for some of the statements he had made following a brief visit to that province. In this case I believe we would do well to recall the old saying, "A man usually finds what he is looking for."
I should like the hon. member for Westmorland to know that I spent several days in his province last spring. I, too, was on a speaking tour, covering parts of Kings, Queens, Victoria and Carleton counties. I was delighted with the country and with the people. The only thing I could not understand was how they were able to drive such fine cars, to have such good homes, wear such good clothes and enjoy such good food-I did enjoy that sea food-on what we in British Columbia would call a very low income. However, they seem to be able to do it, and they deserve credit for it. I believe the people, though, are awakening to the fact that development is badly needed. I believe they feel the government should give and must give more active leadership and direction, so they can develop their wonderful resources and enjoy the benefit of all the good things that are there in such abundance.
I have digressed from my subject. I was going to tell you that in British Columbia we have a very important agricultural industry and, in my riding, we take a back seat to none. A rancher from the Oyama district took a few of his Herefords to the Toronto fair and came back with the championship for fat steers. The 4-H clubs from Armstrong sent contestants to the same fair and came back with the trophy for swine judging. Early in December the co-operative creamery in Vernon processed their millionth pound of butter during the past year. These facts, Mr. Speaker, will show we have a progressive group of farmers.
We have our troubles, too. I was pleased to hear our leader, the hon. member for Peace River, state in this debate a few days ago that we need a plan of flexible- I emphasize that word "flexible"-price supports for basic farm products. I am glad to see that the government is spending millions under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I hope Saskatchewan gets its dam. You
The Address-Mr. McLeod know we have dam troubles in British Columbia too. I still maintain, though, that our province is being discriminated against in that the full provisions of the act are not applicable to us.
I support every vote for funds for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and yet I realize that many changes are necessary to make the assistance fair and equitable. I commend the government for their prompt action in giving financial assistance to the apple growers of Nova Scotia when they suffered such grievous losses last summer. At the same time I condemn the government for their failure to listen to the plea of the Okanagan fruit growers when their orchards and crops were so badly damaged by frost last spring.
I mentioned that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) was in my riding. From all reports he was highly pleased with his reception in Revel-stoke, with the tourist attractions and with the possibility for development that exists there. I can assure the minister that he made a good impression there, too. I am hoping that his promises and proposals for expanding the Revelstoke and Glacier national parks, and improving the facilities for tourists, will be carried out. I think, though, the clear pure air of the district must have gone to his head, for he has since made fantastic proposals that concern us very much. These envision a tunnel to divert part of the water from the great Columbia river into the Fraser watershed.
We in the interior look upon the Columbia as our greatest asset. In fact, we understand that it ranks second to the St. Lawrence itself in power potential. We are anxious to see this great waterway developed. We especially urge that every effort should be made to speed work on the very important Mica creek project, with a progressive plan for other developments. We are suspicious of some of the proposals emanating from Ottawa in recent weeks. We regard this great waterway as a natural resource that belongs, first and last, to the people of the interior of British Columbia. We look upon this as ours, and we look with suspicion on any movement by the federal government to interfere politically with any development that we, the people of British Columbia, feel is in our own best interests.
We have heard much about provincial relations and provincial autonomy in this and the last session. The need for a federal-provincial conference is long overdue. I would urge that before this government takes any

The Address-Mr. McLeod action leading to further interference in provincial rights, the whole matter should be earnestly and quietly discussed around the conference table.
We have heard pleas for greater assistance to road construction. I made such a plea last session, but on this occasion I can do no better than to endorse the words used by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) in this house a few days ago. The trans-Canada highway is of great importance in my constituency and I am anxious to have it completed. I could also talk about assistance for railroads. Despite the fact that this government has turned down every plea for assistance to extend the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, I am glad to see that our provincial government has sufficient courage and initiative to proceed with this great artery into the inland empire of British Columbia and Alberta.
The story of 1954 in British Columbia has been a story of one great achievement after another. I am not narrow enough to place all the credit for this at the feet of the Victoria government, but I will say when encouragement and assistance were needed, and where leadership was required* that government was ready and willing to help out. In spite of the great expenditures for development, the welfare of the people is not being neglected.
When the unemployment problem became serious at the coast, a plea for help was made to Ottawa. I am sorry to say that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) politely told the premier of British Columbia that the province was financially able to look after its own unemployed. Perhaps that is right. We can take care of our own unemployed, but those who flock to the coastal areas, feeling that if they have to go hungry it is the nicest place in Canada in which to be hungry, create a problem that should not be left at the doorstep of charitable organizations or the British Columbia government. I was going to put on the record for this house the words written by the noted columnist the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) dealing with the problem. This was so ably done by my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) the other day that I shall not repeat it. I can only echo his wish that the hon. member for Vancouver South is able to sell his splendid ideas to his government colleagues.
I trust that this government will yet assume their just responsibility toward our unemployed and formulate some plan to remove the problem from our way of life. I would also repeat my plea that this government and the government of British


Columbia get together around the conference table and give the leadership that our people would like to have in developing our resources for the betterment of our province and for Canada as a whole.

speechtext:
In rising to participate in this debate may I be permitted to join with previous speakers in congratulating the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both these newly elected members excelled in their difficult task and offer great promise for the future.
Unlike the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) I was pleased to be reminded in the speech from the throne of the opportunity which was given to the people of Canada of once more extending an affectionate welcome to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother. I was also pleased to hear mentioned the visit of the consort of our sovereign, the Duke of Edinburgh.
Notwithstanding the statements made by numerous speakers from the opposition side of the house, I feel that if one wishes carefully to scrutinize the contents of the speech from the throne he will find concrete evidence of the sound policies of the present government.
In listening to the arguments evolving from some opposition members one would be led to believe that it was the duty of the present government to provide a perpetual scheme of unemployment insurance which, if applied, could easily create a complete disruption in the labour forces of this country. The bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide for an increase in the duration and scale of winter supplementary benefits will be most welcomed by the labour classes of my constituency, where a large proportion of the employment is seasonal. We are given to understand that later on this session a further amendment will be considered, designed to make unemployment insurance a more effective instrument for providing financial support to unemployed workers.
Fishing operations in my constituency are purely of a seasonal nature. It is true that a number of fishermen are owners of their fishing vessels, and it may be a rather difficult problem to have them qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. A larger number, however, are either fishing on wages or are sharing in the gross revenue of their landings. These men are engaged in fishing when employment is available during the summer period. After November 15, or at the latest December 1, fishing operations are curtailed

by ice formations along our shores. At such a time .it is almost impossible for any of these fishermen to secure employment for the winter period. If we are to maintain a flourishing fishing industry, if we want to keep our younger generation interested in following the steps of their forefathers, it is essential that amendments designed to include those fishermen under unemployment benefits be considered at the earliest possible date.
Amendments to the National Housing Act, providing for loans for home improvements, will stimulate further the construction program. I say, Mr. Speaker, at this point that the opening of a Central Mortgage office in the town of Bathurst in my constituency in the spring of 1954 has been most beneficial. From this office alone loans amounting to well over $500,000 have been approved in the first six months of operation. This statement might be a revelation to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) who stated in this house, a few days ago, as reported at page 119 of Hansard:
When you see a new house in certain parts of New Brunswick you really lift up your head to lock because it is something new, whereas in other parts of Canada new houses are a thing of almost everyday occurrence.
If the hon. member visited New Brunswick with the same perception with which he glanced at Montreal and the province of Quebec, no wonder he is concerned with a possibility which could more readily apply to his own district. It is rather difficult for anyone to reconcile the garden of Eden described by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam with the plea for assistance to unemployment presented on the same day by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green).
The introduction of amendments to accelerate the elimination of level crossings will provide additional employment and create further safety measures for our fast growing population.
Legislation providing facilities for loans to fishermen similar to those provided to farmers by the Farm Improvement Loans Act will no doubt create further interest among our fishermen. This legislation, when approved, may not meet with the full approbation or satisfaction of all fishermen; nevertheless I am confident that its application will relieve hardship and provide to a large number a purchasing power which will result in increased efficiency and subsequently in additional earnings.
Reports from a recent fisheries research board annual meeting held in Ottawa indicated the discovery of substantial scallop
The Address-Mr. Robichaud beds in the gulf of St. Lawrence. Fishermen from my constituency have reported in the last few fishing seasons the appearance of scallops along the bay of Chaleur coast and in the proximity of Miscou island. The development of this type of fishery would mean additional revenue to our fishermen and I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that during the 1955 season every effort be undertaken by the fisheries research board to carry on investigations and surveys in the area just mentioned.
The oyster production in New Brunswick reached a record of 37,000 barrels in 1949. Since then this most important fishery has been gradually decreasing from year to year, and when the figures for 1954 are published, I am afraid they will show a further reduction of this variety of shellfish. Oysters are found in the sheltered waters of the southern part of the gulf of St. Lawrence, and only during half the year is the water warm enough for feeding, which causes a slow growth and a limited and uncertain reproduction. It is generally recognized that the natural production of oysters in Canadian waters is not sufficient to meet the demand. It is also an admitted fact that restrictions on the fishing season, on sizes and on the gear to be used do not provide adequate protection for this luxurious shellfish.
Gloucester county is one of the larger oyster producing areas in eastern Canada. Our Shippigan and Caraquet oysters have acquired a nation-wide reputation. It is most urgent that the fisheries research board of Canada, in co-operation with the Department of Fisheries, carry out further investigation to improve the position of this industry. Unless new methods of oyster culture are discovered and large scale trials of cultivation are applied without further delay, I am prepared to predict that within the next five or six years this industry will drop to a new record low, which is causing great concern among our interested oyster fishermen. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Fisheries order an immediate survey of the situation, and that steps be taken at once to expand and improve, if possible, the facilities offered in this connection by the fisheries research board.
Amendments to the veterans welfare legislation or to the War Veterans Allowance Act to raise the basic rates as well as the ceiling on permissible incomes of recipients of allowances will create satisfaction throughout this country.
Early in the year a fire destroyed completely the Keymet mine mill which was at the point of starting its operations. Without losing a single day the management ordered the immediate reconstruction of the destroyed

The Address-Mr. Robichaud structure, and within a few months the new ore concentrator at Keymet was in full operation.
The base metal discoveries of 1953 in the Bathurst area, which were mentioned by the Mining World as the discovery of the year, were further implemented by the remarkable find of American Metal in the adjoining area early in 1954. With the Keymet mine already producing and a second mine ready to resume operation at the site of Brunswick Mining and Smelting, Gloucester county is gradually being recognized as the birthplace of a gigantic new mining field of great significance to the general economy of New Brunswick.
Every effort should be made to see that a zinc smelter, which is urgently needed in eastern Canada, be erected in the logical site offered by Gloucester county. The possible additional secondary industries which may spring up as a result of these new mining discoveries could be equal in importance to the mining and smelting operations. We have to offer in the proximity of these mining sites year-round water shipping facilities unequalled by any base metal mines now operating on Canadian soil. Recent hydrographic surveys have shown that Gloucester county offers facilities for the establishment of a year-round port with sufficient water depth for ocean-going vessels. This factor must not be neglected when the normal development of these mines takes place.
Numerous advantages would be derived if these developments could be followed by the construction of the Chignecto canal. Mineral ores from Ungava could then be processed in Gloucester and follow through this canal the short route to United States outlets.
Unfortunately, at the present time New Brunswick is faced with the major problem of providing adequate cheap power to facilitate the growth and expansion of these newly discovered mines. We have heard recently of the Beechwood project on the Saint John river, and of the possibilities offered by oil shale in Albert county. The water flow of the Saint John river is limited, and even the realization of the Beechwood project will not answer the problem by offering the large block of cheap power needed for the establishment of a flourishing mining industry and the subsidiary or secondary industries which would follow.
I am often wondering if coal, which exists in large quantities in New Brunswick and the neighbouring province of Nova Scotia, has been investigated to its full potentiality as a steam-generating facility. What a boon for the maritime provinces if in the near
[Mr. Robichaud.1
future a method could be found whereby cheap power could be generated from steam. The matter is worth considering and should be studied further by the research council of Canada. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the possibility of the commercial use of atomic energy as a power-generating factor seems to be coming closer to reality. When the day comes when practical use of atomic energy can be applied commercially to generate cheap electric power, may the province of New Brunswick be favoured with the first pilot plant of this kind.
On Friday last I listened with interest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) quoting suggestions made by some hon. members in connection with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river project. Mention has been made of the Canso causeway, of the St. Lawrence seaway, of the trans-Canada highway, of the removal of Ripple Rock and other projects. This reminds me of a most unfortunate situation which exists in the lower end of my constituency of Gloucester. At the northeastern end of the province, with the bay of Chaleur on the west and the gulf of St. Lawrence on the east, are located the islands of Shippigan and Miscou. On the island of Shippigan alone over 5,000 inhabitants are living who depend almost entirely on fishing for a livelihood. The distance from the island to the mainland is slightly over half a mile and transportation consists of a cable ferry. Unfortunately, during the winter months the operation of the ferry is prevented by heavy ice formations, and these island residents have to use the ice bridge to communicate with the mainland. During the freeze-up period in late fall, and during the moving of ice in the spring, these poor inhabitants are left for weeks at a time without communication with the mainland. Those who have decided to take risks on insecure ice blocks have taken chances which, in many instances, have resulted in loss of life.
The cost of construction of a bridge to the mainland is greatly increased on account of navigation which has to pass through this channel. The entire Gloucester county fishing fleet uses this passage on its way to and returning from the fishing banks. This necessitates an open span or a bridge with an overhead clearance of approximately 40 feet at high tide. In view of these being navigable waters, I would suggest that the federal government consider the possibility of contributing its share to assure the construction of a bridge between Shippigan island and the mainland, thus relieving this unfortunate population of hardship and unnecessary worry.

(Translation):
As one of the representatives of French Acadian origin in the house, may I be permitted, at the beginning of this memorable year 1955, to salute, in my mother tongue, my French Acadian compatriots who this year celebrate the second centenary of the deportation of 1755.
The celebration of the second centenary of the deportation of the Acadians will mark an epoch in Canadian history. Mr. Speaker, the members of the house may rest assured that it is not our intention to revive a certain resentment brought about by a sad and unfortunate period of our people's history, but rather to mark officially and solemnly the rebirth and the survival of a small group who, exactly two centuries ago, had been condemned to dispersal and to almost certain destruction.
History tells us that out of some 15,000 to
16,000	people who had been deported in 1755, fathers, mothers and children of all ages banished from their homes, 6,000 to 7,000 only survived the innumerable hardships and miseries that were to be their lot. Through a miracle that cannot be ascribed to any earthly power, those few thousand exiles, that martyred people of the past, multiplied and rose again with such a determination to survive that they succeeded in overcoming the numerous obstacles which threatened their miraculous survival.
The descendants of that small people, banished and dispersed as a result of the "great disturbance", number today, after two centuries, more than 1J million. Almost 300,000 Acadian descendants now live in the maritime provinces. Another 300,000 are scattered over the Gaspe peninsula and other parts of the province of Quebec. We find 100,000 of them and even more in the New England states and more than half a million have settled in Louisiana. In my own constituency, I am happy to be able to salute some 50,000 people of French Acadian origin who will take part with me, this year, in the celebration of our second centenary.
At the very moment when I am addressing this house, an impressive delegation of 135 members from Quebec province and the mari-times are being officially entertained at Alexandria, Lafayette, Baton Rouge and, more precisely today, at New Orleans. Nearly half a million descendants of these unfortunate exiles of 1755 now live in these Louisiana cities and towns. Those who, through destitution, difficulties, demoralization, perhaps,
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
were prevented from making their way back to the forsaken land of Acadia chose that corner of the North American continent, wherein they had been carried by wind and wave, to make for themselves a new country.
With faith in God and Providence, the Acadians have retained the customs and traditions of their ancestors, as well as that gentle tongue of which, even now, you may be able to notice some overtones. Our Acadian people live in complete understanding with Canadians of British and other origins. They are peaceful and brotherly people, proud of their revealing survival and of their long and arduous rise to a place in the sun. The Acadian has preserved his love for the evergreen forest and his attraction for the almost enchanting and hypnotic breath of the ocean which offers him also the sight of the sun rising and setting magnificently in its glorious waters. This love for the sea and for the forest perhaps explains the irresistible propensity of the Acadian to seek a place close to the ocean. These sons of the exiled have become fishermen unfearful of the offing and unmindful of the hardships of the climate and storms, and are admittedly unequalled when it comes to felling trees in virgin forests.
Years, generations, have passed. Acadia, which was deemed forever destroyed, carried on patiently her reconstruction in the background. By a seldom empty cradle, the Acadian mother continued, and still does, to hum the old French songs and keeps on teaching persistently faith in God and respect for the authority. The cradle of the Acadian family is perhaps the secret of this miraculous survival.
In the cultural and social fields, the awakening and the progress are perhaps more obvious still. In the maritimes, Acadia today has her colleges and her universities: Ste. Anne college, at Church Point, in Nova Scotia; St. Joseph University in Memramcook, with its extension in Moncton; Sacred Heart University in Bathurst and St. Louis College in Edmundston. Notre Dame d'Acadie College for girls and several convents provide our young generation with a solid education based on principles which safeguard our language and our faith.
Today Acadia has, in the religious sphere, its archbishop, its bishops and a goodly number of priests, brothers and nuns. In the political field we are proud that one of Acadia's sons became the premier of a province, while some others have represented us

The Address-Mr. Nowlan creditably in the federal cabinet. We have our own judges, our own lawyers, our own doctors and our own engineers; we have in every profession representatives of whom we can be proud. We have also, in Acadia, our own French radio station and our own mutual insurance association, the Assumption Society. In the industrial and commercial sphere, our own people have forged ahead and now hold the foremost place in many branches of that field.
In a few weeks, to commemorate the bicentenary, one of our colleagues in this house, the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault), who is descended from that race which would not die, will honour us with a book bearing a most appropriate title: h'Acadie des Ancetres. That book will throw more light on the genealogy of the early Acadian families. In simple and easy language, the author will strive to bring back to life, in these few pages, the names of the founders and pioneers of the Acadia of bygone days. We will see names like Arsenault, Boudreau, Boucher, Chiasson, Doucet, Dugas, LeBlanc, Landry, Leger, LeBouthillier, LeBreton, LeMenager, Melanson, Michaud, Poirier, Richard, Roy, Robichaud, Savoie, Veniot and many others whom it would take too long to mention.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saluting this definite revival of the Acadian people. May Acadia be ever prosperous and keep on progressing towards the achievement of her destinies on American soil.
Before resuming my seat, on behalf of my compatriots I tender an official invitation to the Canadian people at large to take part in the magnificent celebrations that will mark the second centenary next summer at Grand Pre, Moncton, Caraquet and many other centres of the maritimes and Quebec. We also hope that the Canadian government will take part, in a concrete manner, in the celebration of the second centenary of the deportation of 1755.
