speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on the address is, of course, one of the two parliamentary milestones; the mountains, you might say, we climb as the session progresses. The other one is the debate on the budget during which theoretically every citizen through the mouth of his member of parliament can present his or her grievances.
But this occasion, I am afraid, is looked upon by many as something of a bore. They forget the fact that the history behind this address in reply to the speech from the

throne goes back to the very foundation of our constitution. They also forget that men risked their freedom and indeed their lives to make sure the executive, which presents its demands in writing before parliament, is made to account for those demands, and that through this means members of parliament now have a right to present their own views before dealing with those of the executive.
It is true, I am prepared to admit, that this principle might sometimes be abused. We have perhaps seen examples of that abuse in this house on more than one occasion. On the other hand we also see examples, as we did last week, of how parliament can deal with important or emergency matters efficiently and within a few hours.
It is therefore much better that members of parliament be permitted to bring too many things before the house than that they be curtailed in any manner. We sometimes hear suggestions that discussion should be curtailed, but I for one would oppose any such curtailment with all the power I can command.
It is conventional on these occasions to congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think perhaps, as they do in the United States congress, it would be more efficient if we took that as read and passed on to something else. Nevertheless, having gone through that experience myself in a different place, and knowing something of the trial it is to a new member, I wish to join with those who have gone before in extending my congratulations to the two hon. gentlemen who performed a very difficult task in a most exceptional manner.
If I may be permitted a personal word, I would also like to welcome into this house another new member, namely the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Richardson) . I would have preferred to see another member enter the house on the behalf of the Progressive Conservative party, but if there has to be another Liberal here I am very glad it is the hon. member I have mentioned because after all he is a Nova Scotian, a graduate of Acadia and of the Dalhousie law school. With that background I am quite sure he will overcome the handicap of belonging to the political party of which he is now a member and make a real contribution to the debates in this house.
I am also glad to welcome the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler). Most of us do not know him very well. If you go into the office of your bank manager you wonder when he stares at you just what kind of

glass eye he has, and whether you will succeed in arousing his sympathy. But the new Minister of Transport seems very human, and he sat for many years in another place similar to ours. He must have made requests to the government and had the feeling of being frustrated and denied. He will therefore have a good deal of sympathy for those who make requests from this side of the house, and I can assure him we will exercise our right to make such appeals.
Since he is now here-and I do not mean that he is not always in his place-I wish to bring to his attention one matter in the speech from the throne which bothers me a great deal. Before I do that, however, as I am going to indulge in a word or two of criticism, perhaps I had better for the time being maintain this atmosphere of kindliness and good will.
There is another matter to which I want to make reference and which is referred to in the speech from the throne, namely the damage done to Nova Scotia by "Hurricane Edna." In that connection I want to express my appreciation and that of the people whom I represent to this government for the sympathy and practical co-operation which they extended to the fruit growers of the Annapolis valley. It is a devastating and terrifying thing to see what happened in this valley, which survived the vicissitudes of the war and while not perhaps overcoming the exchange difficulties, nevertheless faced them and brought the orchards back again into production with the finest apple crop which has ever been produced down there; I do not mean the largest, but the finest.
With the prospect of the British market opening up, and with harvesting only a few days away, in a few short hours we saw 60, 70 or 80 per cent of the crop thrown to the ground, when everyone's credit was extended to the very limit in the effort to bring that industry back as it was being brought back.
That was the situation we faced. As I said before, I want to express my appreciation to the government and particularly to the minister from Nova Scotia and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), with whom I dealt on various occasions during that time and who always showed the greatest interest in this matter. I know the people greatly appreciate what was done.
I should also like to pay a tribute to the efficiency of the officials of the Department of Agriculture who went down to that valley and handled a situation which was, to say the least, rather novel. Karl Conger and others went down from here and within a few short days they evolved a system which was
The Address-Mr. Nowlan hammered out by trial and error, but it was more trial and less error than one would expect; it worked exceptionally well. As a result, instead of a disaster which could have completely wiped out the fruit industry of Nova Scotia, at least we were able to survive and the people there can look to the future at least with courage, if not with too much optimism.
In that connection I think I should say also that although we suffered severely, two or three weeks afterwards when we read of the disaster which occurred in Ontario and of the terrible loss of life in and around Toronto, we realized how fortunate we had been in that our loss was entirely material and not both material and physical, such as that which was suffered elsewhere.
As I have already said, there is one matter in the speech from the throne that I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler). Dealing with the ferry service, the speech from the throne reads as follows:
It is expected that, in the course of the coming season, the new ferry between North Sydney and Port aux Basques will be in operation and the ferry service between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor started.
Ordinarily one would pass by that paragraph without question. But having dealt with this matter for six years now and having followed the many statements with respect to this ferry during that period, I am wondering whether there is a play on words being made between "being in operation" and "started". This ferry, Mr. Speaker, has started and stopped more often than any other ship ever built, not excluding Noah's ark, and its history goes back almost as far. I went to the trouble of getting extracts from statements made by the minister-I am not going to weary the house by going into details; it was not the present minister, of course, but his predecessor and other ministers-dealing with the course of construction of this boat. The story of Alice in Wonderland has nothing whatsoever on this story. When the minister speaks I hope he will tell us what is the difference between being in operation and starting. We do not want this one to stop. We want it to start and not stop. It has been a matter of stopping and starting up until now.
Away back in 1949 the then minister read an official statement in which he said this boat would be completed in time for the 1951 tourist season. Let me just interject this remark with regard to tourists. I think perhaps too much emphasis is laid on the fact that this is supposed to be a ferry for the benefit of tourists and, therefore, of course,

The Address-Mr. Novolan for the benefit of our economy. It is true that we are tremendously interested in the tourist industry. It is true that we hope this ferry will accommodate hundreds and thousands of tourists coming into the maritime provinces. But there is much more to it than that, Mr. Speaker.
In Nova Scotia, particularly perhaps in my own constituency in the Annapolis valley, we grow large quantities of small fruits, such as strawberries, cherries, peaches and fruits of that kind. We need access to the United States market. We need access to Boston and New York. With that ferry in operation and operating on a proper schedule, we shall be able to put refrigerated trucks or even ordinary commercial trucks out of the valley and into the Boston market within a few hours.
This matter is therefore of importance to more than the tourist industry. It is important to the farmers. It is important to the fishermen. They are all getting fed up with the delays which have characterized this service. As I said before, we were promised it in 1951. Incidentally, I may say that we were then told that its cost would be $3 million, of which Nova Scotia would pay $1,500,000. The province drove a fairly good bargain and agreed to pay not more than $1,500,000 or 50 per cent, whichever was the lesser. I notice the figure is now over $5,100,000. The cost is certainly much greater than anticipated. From the standpoint of economy, I hope the minister will get this boat going fairly soon. Otherwise the cost may run up to $9 or $10 million.
As I said before, the whole thing has been a comedy of errors. After he said it would be ready in 1951, and then in 1952, we were told it could not be built because of the shortage of steel. Yet two days after the minister made that announcement that it could not be built because of the shortage of steel he went into his own constituency-as, of course, he had a right to do; he was the member for that constituency-and announced that the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway was to be commenced at once. It did not get commenced at once, I must say; but it did not add to the good feeling in the province of Nova Scotia to be told that a boat which would take a few hundred tons of steel could not be proceeded with because we did not have the steel, but that we were going to proceed at once with the construction of another public work which would take infinitely larger quantities of steel.
Finally we arrived at the stage where they were going to let the contract, Mr. Speaker. Apparently the contractor had some suspicion with regard to the plans. The ship was to


have a speed of 18J knots, I think. After the naval architect for the department had prepared the plans, the contractor said he was not satisfied, and that he wanted a model. A model was made, and it was then found that the ship could not attain the speed which had been ordered, and also that it did not have the required stability. I understand that is a euphemism for saying that it could not go ahead and that, if it did go ahead, it would upset. Let us remember that this boat was to traverse some of the roughest water in the world. So again there was delay. The matter has been delayed and delayed until finally it is actually coming under the aegis of the present minister, although of course he is not responsible for it.
We heard there was to be a launching. All the preparations were made for it. The government bought a bottle of champagne. They wrapped it up in fancy tissue paper; I have no doubt about that. A very charming lady was chosen to break the bottle of champagne over the bow. A silk cord was bought by means of which to swing the bottle to be smashed against the bow. Then somebody started to think perhaps they had better look into the ship in order to find out what was in it. When they did so, what do you think they found? They found they had forgotten to order the worm gears for the engine. Therefore there was no use in launching it, because if they launched it they would not be able to get it out of port. They checked up and found that the order had not gone to Great Britain for the worm gears; and that worm gears were supposed to have been ordered over a year ago. Worm gears, incidentally, are not little bits of things. They are what transfer the power from the engine to the shaft. So the matter has been delayed again. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) looks at me incredulously but these, sir, are facts that can be established. The champagne will keep, of course.

The champagne is in Montreal, not Nova Scotia. I thought, without being uncharitable or unkind, is that not somewhat in keeping with Liberal promises and Liberal performance? They buy their champagne but they forget to buy the worm gears. I hate to disillusion so early a new minister coming into the house, but I want to assure him that if he has been reading the press clippings of his department or of his colleagues and has believed them he is in for sad disillusionment, so we might as well disillusion him right now.

Incidentally, we had an election in Nova Scotia in 1953, and part of the Liberal publicity at that time was a full-page advertisement showing this steamer cruising across the sheets of the Halifax Herald with a bone in her teeth. She must have been making 15 or 20 knots an hour. This was one of the performances of the government on the basis of which they asked for re-election.
When I look at the statement the minister made last year, which I did not read analytically until today, I find something that is rather mysterious. The contract was signed on December 31, 1953. What the contract was for I do not know, because the keel was laid on July 30, 1953 and the launching took place on November 8, 1953. It was launched about six months after the election, but still it was launched some considerable time before the contract was let. It is no wonder the contractor has had difficulties about the matter.
I think the minister will perhaps understand now why I am slightly concerned about what has happened. We down there in the east want some assurance about this matter, because I can tell the minister that the public are angry and frustrated with respect to it. To be fair in that connection, and I want to be fair, I should also add that so far as the construction of the Canso causeway is concerned, it has been proceeded with expeditiously and efficiently. I think a very good job was done which will be of service to the province and for which due congratulations should be given.
Since the minister is in the house, and because he has sat in opposition, and because I know he is a sympathetic man and will listen at least with patience to the pleas of the opposition, even if repeated, I can perhaps trespass on the good nature of the house to make one other plea which I have made before. I ask him to discuss with his departmental officials the inauguration of a coastguard service on the Atlantic coast. The other day the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) made this suggestion with respect to the great lakes. I have no doubt it was a sound and proper suggestion, but I can assure him it is even more justified in so far as the Atlantic coast is concerned. The minister's predecessor always listened sympathetically, shook his head and said it was not necessary and could not be done. He said the search and rescue squadron of the R.C.A.F. was now performing functions which obviated the necessity for a coastguard service.
I do not want to depreciate one little bit the services of the search and rescue squadron. It is based in my constituency, and I know what these men do; but aeroplanes cannot land on rough waters and high seas.
The Address-Mr. Nowlan The minister from the province knows full well, because he comes from a maritime constituency where men go down to the sea in ships, that every year boat after boat comes drifting ashore, boats that have been lost for days. The men are either dying or sometimes even dead, and the evidence is all too plain that they have died within the last few hours. If some kind of co-ordinated search could have been made their lives would have been saved.
I do not think it would amount to a tremendous expenditure. I do not know, of course, but there are many ships in the department. There are the fisheries inspection ships and so on. There is the search and rescue squadron. I think what is needed largely is co-ordination and direction. We are in the position down there that when we need help we have to appeal to the United States coastguard service. I must say that it, of course, is one of the most efficient coastguard services, I presume the most efficient in the world. It has rendered yeoman service, but one does not always want to be applying to the Americans for help, and it is very often difficult for them to render that help anyway. We are told that we have to go to the NATO pool for shipping and that we have to go to the United States for coastguard service. I doubt if that is fitting for a maritime nation such as our own. I hope the minister will take this request under consideration again, and see if something can be done to inaugurate a coastguard service. It is badly needed, will serve a most useful purpose and, as I said, I think without too much additional expense.
There is another minister who has changed places since we spoke last in the house. He has not sat in opposition, but I should like to renew to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) an appeal I have made on different occasions and which I am going to continue to make as long as the present situation exists. I am asking that the question of grants to universities be reviewed and reconsidered, and that the system be amended by the government. As far as the grants themselves are concerned, I believe we all commend the government for them. I think we recognize that today universities are playing a more and more important role in the life of the nation, and that to some extent at any rate they are a national responsibility.
Without universities our industrial and scientific production, even our civil service, would not be able to function. All one has to do is look at the advertisements appearing from day to day for men for the civil service to see the emphasis which is placed upon university graduation. Yet the universities are caught, as everyone else is, with higher
254	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nowlan costs. Because of high taxation and succession duties the beneficent gifts of the old days, the large, substantial donations, have unfortunately decreased and in many cases virtually disappeared, leaving the universities with reduced funds.
The problem is an increasingly difficult one. Universities today are financed more and more on the tuition fees charged students. The problem has increased alarmingly in the last few years. It is a problem, of course, which I am sure the government will have to look at in a far wider field within the next five to ten years, because we are just on the verge of a new problem with respect to universities. Everyone realizes that between 1960 and 1965 we are going to commence to get the influx of students who were born at the time of the wartime prosperity increased birth rate. The physical plant of every university will be taxed to the limit. The faculties will be taxed. Facilities will have to be increased tremendously, but in the meantime they have not had the financial backing to maintain their present operation, let alone the expansion with which they will be confronted. I know that presents a national problem of far greater financial significance than the one I am mentioning at the moment.
To come back to the present, what is the situation? I think most hon. members are conversant with it. The dominion government makes available to the provinces 50 cents per head of population. Then the province distributes the money among its approved colleges. That at least is an advance over getting no assistance whatsoever. But how does it work out?
In the province of Nova Scotia we have a relatively small population for which we get 50 cents a head, and that money is made available to the universities. We have several universities in the province. Some will say that we have too many, but their roots are in the ground, they are established, they have rendered service to this country and are going to continue to render that service. We have no state university whatsoever in the province of Nova Scotia. None of the universities of the province get provincial grants at all, as is the case in most of the other provinces of Canada.
We do have professional schools in Halifax, and at Dalhousie we have law, medicine, dentistry and pharmacy which attract students from all over the maritime provinces and beyond. I know that in my son's class, the third year in law at Dalhousie, there are ten students from Ontario this year. The Nova Scotia technical college attracts engineering


students from Mount Allison and the University of New Brunswick as well as other places. They are all charged up against the per capita payment to Nova Scotia.
I am not going to deal with the situation in detail, Mr. Speaker, but I communicated with the Department of Finance today and in these figures I have given you illustrations of how the existing system operates. In Newfoundland the university gets $477 per student because that province has only one college, as I understand it, and the registration apparently is not too large. I believe they have 401 students. At 50 cents per head of population they get $191,500 or $477 per student in that college. Prince Edward Island gets $209 per student, and then these grants drop down. Those are the two highest. Ontario gets $144 per student, Alberta $158 per student, and then there are three, Mr. Speaker, below $125.
In Nova Scotia this year, according to the department, we are going to receive only $89 per student as compared with $477 in Newfoundland and $209 in Prince Edward Island. Manitoba will get $10 more, or $99 per student. British Columbia, which apparently has a tremendous student body of 5,616, will receive only $109 per student. You have, therefore, three provinces in Canada that will receive less than $125 per student.
I have made this suggestion before, Mr. Speaker, and I am urging it again. As I said, we have a new Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) who knows something of the experience of smaller universities. I know there are others in the government who have experience with universities. I am urging again that the government maintain the present system if that is their desire, but on the basis of a guaranteed payment of $125 per student as a minimum, or 50 cents a head. In that case the grants will be increased for only three provinces, Nova Scotia, British Columbia and Manitoba. The total involved will be relatively small, but it will make a substantial difference to the universities in those provinces.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, it will make a tremendous difference to the universities in Nova Scotia, where we now feel we are carrying a burden for all of eastern Canada. As a result we get the smallest grant of any province in Canada.
I am wandering somewhat afield on these matters, and I want to shift to another matter about which I have been intrigued during the last little while as the result of reading a series of articles which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. There has been some discussion about this matter pre-

viously. I want to bring it before the house at this time, and I am not suggesting any solution. I do not know what the solutions are. I believe there is something here to which we should be paying attention. I refer to the problem of the British West Indies vis-a-vis the Dominion of Canada. At one time the British West Indies was one of our greatest markets. A man sitting within the sound of my voice at this moment said earlier in the day that ordinarily he shipped thousands of bushels of potatoes to the West Indies, but this year not a bushel is going down there. In 1947 our exports to the West Indies amounted to over $80 million. Then foreign exchange control was imposed by Britain and the dollars dried up. Their purchases have fallen off until they are now less than $40 million.
I suggest that is not a matter this government has anything to do with at all, but is a matter of foreign exchange control restrictions imposed by the British government. Last year I went to a board which is administered here by the Department of Trade and Commerce, for the sterling stabilization fund for the West Indies. I went on behalf of a constituent who wanted to ship
10,000	boxes of apples to the West Indies. Finally, after making many calls-that was not the fault of the officials-that board was able to provide enough dollars to enable us to ship 2,000 boxes down there. As I said, there was a market for 10,000 boxes.
I feel this example could be multiplied a dozen times. Perhaps I am interested in the problem because the West Indies market has always had a traditional significance for the maritimes. In the days of our old wooden ships we took our potatoes, lumber and fish to the West Indies and brought back fruit, molasses and spices.

speechtext: And rum.

speechtext:
Yes, we also brought back rum; there is no question about that. It was a very profitable trade, and I am told it was good rum. Before my day that trade dried up, so I cannot tell you about that. This trade was perhaps the background of the economic development of the maritime provinces; but as I said, it has almost entirely disappeared today. If something could be done to revive these markets it would be of direct assistance to the maritimes and Canada as a whole would benefit. I think there is a real problem there, Mr. Speaker.
Those of us who have been to the West Indies are somewhat shocked and appalled by the conditions which exist there. There is more food and yet probably more people verging on starvation there than any place
The Address-Mr. Nowlan in the world. You have people who are discontented, unhappy, poverty-stricken, living in hovels and in many cases under intolerable conditions. We are worrying about communism, and properly so. We have tried to assist in the Far East and in the Near East. We have our Colombo plan to which I give full support, and which I think should be extended even farther. I am wondering if we have not a problem right on our own doorstep which perhaps requires something of a Colombo plan. Something must be done because after all, without becoming an alarmist, every day we hear rumours. We know that only a little while ago there was trouble in different parts of the Caribbean.
You have a field there which is ripe for communism or anything else if something is not done in the relatively near future. The situation demands attention. I feel we should be giving some attention to that, and not merely because of the spread of communism. Whether it is in the form of a commercial union, whether it is in the form of financial assistance of some kind such as a miniature West Indies Colombo plan, or whatever the solution may be, there is a problem which is crying for attention. We are going to be forced to give it attention in the not too distant future, from the standpoint of national defence or any other way you want to look at it.
It is true that tourists go down there and create wealth; they bring money into the country. However, this also creates antagonism, especially when you see people flippantly throwing coins into the water for which the boys dive, and when they come back that is their penny for the day. This does not help create the good will which we are prone to boast about. I suggest some attention must be paid to this problem in the not distant future.
One could go over the problems which have been stressed by other members here. I do not propose to do that. We had a speech the other day by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) emphasizing the problem of the coal industry. I could echo everything he said, and at a later date I intend to deal with that problem, but not at this time. Then there is the problem of agriculture. It is trite to say that agriculture is depressed. It is proper to say that. Of course there are many examples, individual ones, that point to the contrary.
I am not going to subscribe to all the theories that have been advanced for the solution of agricultural problems, but I think increased production and efficiency will go a long way to meeting them if we have markets

The Address-Mr. Nowlan available for our products. Take our own fruit industry. One man with a power pruner attached to a power sprayer will prune more acres of orchard in a day than a dozen could do in a week a few years ago. In a day one power sprayer will spray more efficiently a larger acreage of orchard than formerly would be sprayed by four or five men in a week. Today the small unit, as in so many other branches of agriculture, is rapidly passing, from the standpoint of being an efficient producer. But unless you have markets, Mr. Speaker, the situation is really serious.
Although this government could be commended for things it has done

it could be commended for the extension of the war veterans' allowance, for the disabled pensions and a few things like that-I wonder whether the speech from the throne does show the vision, the imagination and the courage which are necessary to deal with the problems facing Canada today.
They talk about blasting Ripple Rock. I am sure that is of great importance to the people of British Columbia. It brings much satisfaction to my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). But I think it is the first time I can recall that constitutionally such language has been put in the mouth of the representative of His Majesty or Her Majesty-that a rock was to be blasted. When I read the speech it appeared to me that somebody had started optimistically with the first paragraph and the last paragraph, and had hoped to put something very important in between; but then something happened and they could not, so they just filled it in with this and that. Whether I am right in that I do not know. But Ripple Rock is there; the constitutional rock which threatened confederation was not mentioned. Perhaps that was obviated this afternoon. We shall see when we have an opportunity of reading the papers in connection with it.
I suggest kindly it is indicative of the approach which is being made by this government to the problems of today. There is nothing there which indicates the government is going to face the crisis confronting agricultural production and other problems.
I was intrigued by the C.C.F. amendment. It said that the government had gone back to uncontrolled and unrestricted free enterprise. When was there ever unrestricted and uncontrolled free enterprise in this country, Mr. Speaker? This nation historically has always been a nation of compromises. We were a small nation with a thin population strung north of the 49th parallel. From the beginning we had to compromise. We built the Canadian Pacific Railway with government assistance; then having built a so-called

private railway, we afterwards took over a public one and operated it in competition with the private railway. We have a privately owned radio industry and a national broadcasting system as well. In no country in the world has there been a greater degree of successful compromise evolved between private enterprise and the state. In that way we are evolving, perhaps slowly, certainly not colourfully, not dramatically, a distinct Canadian nation with a distinctly Canadian culture and background. It is certainly not one of unrestricted and uncontrolled free enterprise, I can assure you of that; but I do think that we are perhaps not facing up to other problems.
I am intrigued by my hon. friends on the left talking about raising the old age pension to $65 a month. One can have sympathy with a proposition such as that. One knows that it is made sincerely, but I wonder when in this country we are going to create an atmosphere in which there will not always be pie in the sky for someone. I was rather shocked a little while ago when I received a letter from a constituent who told me he had his gall bladder out, and he now wanted a gall bladder pension. I presume that other hon. members have had the same experience. I think the time has come when in this country we have to produce more, and realize that there is no pie in the sky for all.
I do believe that the speech from the throne does not face this situation at all. It was written in a sort of languorous attitude on a late summer afternoon with the shadows of the setting sun falling across the page of the speech that was being written. It was not written in the bright, crisp sunlight of the early morning, when inspiration and action would be demanded.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the subamendment. I do not want to indulge in any unnecessary verbosity and repeat the excellent arguments put forward by a number of speakers in this group in support of our criticisms and various proposals, but I wish to make a few comments this afternoon.
I must say I personally was very pleased indeed to learn that there are going to be improvements in the war veterans allowance, and I am sure we all await with great interest the introduction of the bill. The announcement of those improvements have'been very cheering words to many veterans and their dependents. We are also glad to note that the government is giving notice of the reestablishment of the veterans affairs committee. Once again, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a plea that this committee be made a permanent committee of this house.

It could be a clearing house lor veterans problems and administration problems generally, and it would offer advantages not only to the opposition but to the minister and the government.
I was also very pleased to see the amendment to the Blind Persons Act, to lower the age of eligibility and raise the income ceilings. I am sure that measure will be welcomed by all hon. members. I was also pleased to see the suggestion that there would be an amendment to the Railway Act to accelerate the elimination of level crossings. Many members have for years been advocating a more vigorous policy on the part of the government with respect to the removal of the dangerous railroad crossings in this country.
Then two other very interesting measures are amendments to the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, and a measure to control works which will affect the normal flow of rivers across international boundaries. These measures are of great importance to Canadians as a whole. I am sure when they are under discussion they will create great national interest. They are of great importance to British Columbia, and of particular importance to the people whom I represent.
I intend to speak at some length when these bills are under discussion, but I wish now to make a few comments on certain remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), when he spoke in the debate on Wednesday, January 12. At page 114 of Hansard, when referring to these measures, the hon. member had this to say:
Insofar as the plans of the government with regard to the Columbia river system are concerned, we approve of anything which means the use of Canadian resources by the Canadian people.
That is just what the government intends to provide for. The hon. member went on:
But I am afraid the story is not quite that simple.
I believe this proposal is also designed as a club with which to beat the government of the province of British Columbia.
Later, on the same page and in the same speech the hon. member said:
There must be co-operation between the two governments. I believe that both sides are sincere.
It seems to me a strictly illogical position to take to suggest that the government is using this legislation to beat the government of British Columbia over the head, and at the same time impute motives to that government which the hon. member considers to be sincere on this question.
I just want to say a word or two along this line because there has been some suggestion in the country that the government is acting unfairly, and I mention this because 50433-17
The Address-^-Mr. Herridge I am particularly anxious to see this question discussed on its merits. I am not a supporter of the government of British Columbia, and I am not a supporter of the government of Canada. However, I think this matter is so important that we should not have the whole situation fogged with the misunderstanding that it is purely a partisan and political matter.
United States interests have been very interested in the building of this dam since 1947. It has been discussed in congressional committees and by the Columbia basin committee of the United States; and it has been discussed by a good number of senators. In 1948 the United States Columbia basin commission passed the following resolution, which I quote to prove a point or two:
Resolved by the Columbia basin commission that it hereby requests the international joint commission to direct its international board of engineers to give priority to studies and report on the storage of water in Arrow lakes, British Columbia, so that the commission may decide the amount of storage it will approve there, and if such report be favourable, that the Bonneville power administration and the United States, and the proper governmental agency of British Columbia and Canada, then proceed to negotiate for an agreement.
My first point is that in their resolution the commission recognizes the chain of responsibility-the international joint commission, the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia. Then the resolution goes on to say:
-and be it further resolved, that the commission urge the state legislature, the members of congress from Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Montana, the governors of said states, and the President of the United States, to join in the above request to the American members of the international joint commission and the premier of British Columbia and the Prime Minister of Canada to join in the above request to the Canadian members of the international joint commission in the hope that the threatened electrical catastrophe to the Pacific northwest during the next five years may be averted, and that, instead, both the United States and Canada may have increased development and prosperity and a stronger national defence.
I quote that resolution to indicate that the chain of responsibility on this question is recognized by governmental authorities in the United States.
I remember discussing this matter in 1949 with the late Mr. J. Webster, a member of the Liberal party and the member for the constituency of Rossland-Trail, who strongly urged the coalition government of British Columbia to conduct an investigation as a result of this request of the United States for the building of a low level dam on the Arrow lakes for storage purposes.

The Address-Mr. Herridge
I am informed that the government of British Columbia did consider the matter, but after discussing it with other bodies and receiving technical advice and so on they decided not to proceed with it as they felt it was not in the best interests of British Columbia to proceed with the proposal. I mention this to indicate that the matter has been discussed before, and I am quite sure it is only fair to say that the attitude on the part of the government at this time in relation to this question is simply the continuation of an attitude that has existed throughout the years.
The attitude of the Canadian section of the international joint commission is indicated in a speech by General McNaughton to the Pacific northwest trade association, delivered at Spokane, Washington, on November 2, 1953, before these proposals ever came before the house. In connection with this suggested low level dam General McNaughton had this to say:
As regards the storage on the Arrow lakes which was mentioned this morning, the project is very much in the mind of our engineering board, but it ranks less in possibility of over-all benefit from a basin point of view and very much less in possible benefit to Canada and in consequence we are giving priority to the Mica project.
This matter was also under discussion in the external affairs committee last session, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked General McNaughton the following question which I find in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the external affairs committee, No. 7, dated May 12, 1954 at page 175:
Q. The actual construction could not be done until you people have approved?
A. No, sir.
I just mention these facts because I for one am very interested in seeing that this whole question be discussed in a purely objective way, since the matters being decided concerning the Columbia river are of great importance to the people of British Columbia, and are of particular importance to the people I have the honour to represent. I would like to say further that many hon. members do not recognize the fact that if it had not been for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) turning down the request to divert Yukon waters to Skagway for the production of power for the production of aluminum, British Columbia would not now be having the opportunity to consider the Frobisher proposals.
I think under the circumstances it is not fair to suggest that the legislation proposed in the speech from the throne with regard to the control of waters flowing across the

international boundary is designed as a club with which to beat the government of British Columbia.
Before leaving that argument I simply wish to say that as a result of the public interest in this question-and I intend to say quite a bit more on it at a later date-I hope there will be a meeting of minds, as General McNaughton put it on one occasion, between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia, and that we can get together to develop the great Columbia river to our common and mutual advantage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we took recess for dinner I was bringing to the attention of the house and of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) the fact that while this government has a policy of trying to persuade private employers to employ as many older people as possible, some departments were not giving effect to that policy. I read a letter which had been written to me by the chairman of the civil service commission in which he pointed out that the second reason for difficulty in applying the policy was the willingness or unwillingness of departmental officials to accept for employment veterans whose term of employment would be relatively short.
I want to protest most emphatically about the unwillingness of departmental officers to give effect to a policy that the government and the Department of Labour are urging private employers to accept. I hope there may be some remedy to this situation, and that we shall not have this buck-passing from the civil service commission to the officers of the various departments and back to the Minister of Labour. It is a serious situation because it means there are a good number of capable older people who could be satisfactorily employed, particularly in the lighter civil service positions, who are being denied that opportunity actually against the announced policy of this government.
I have just a couple of items still to deal with, Mr. Speaker. I am making to some extent what Mr. Michael Barkway would call one of my parochial speeches, which deal with local matters, but they are of serious concern to my constituents.
* I understand that the government is giving consideration to the sale of certain veteran rental housing projects that have been established across Canada. One of these projects, namely the Sunningdale veterans housing project, is in my constituency. Of course, in giving consideration to the sale, they are giving consideration to the price. I have been informed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that the contract price for the construction of these houses was $5,200 for a two-bedroom house and $5,800 for a three-bedroom house. I have made inquiries, and I find that the city of Trail has

The Address-Mr. Mclvor
assessed the two-bedroom house at $1,900 and the three-bedroom house at $2,100. Those assessments are on the basis of 60 per cent of replacement value. Those assessments have been approved by the provincial equalization board of British Columbia as being in line with standard practice and values.
The government has had rent from those houses for some years. They have had certain maintenance and administrative costs. But in addition to that, the veteran purchasers of those homes spent, in the majority of cases, considerable sums in improving the grounds around the houses, making fills and doing landscaping, planting and so on. Some of them have made extensive repairs and improvements to these houses. I urge that the minister give consideration to all these facts, when the sale price is being considered.
I understand that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not operated for profit. I make a strong appeal that these houses be sold to these veterans in Canada at the net cost to the government at the time of the sale. I am sure such a policy would receive the support of the majority of the members of this house. The government would not be losing a cent. They would simply be selling houses to these veterans at the net cost at the time of sale.
I mention this matter because some of these veterans are somewhat disturbed at the prices they hear they might be expected to pay. For the life of me I cannot see why Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should expect to make a dollar out of projects such as these. I am sure the people of Canada would be well pleased if these men receive these houses at the cost to the government at the time of sale.
Before leaving this question of housing I want to say that I listened to the extremely interesting speech the other day by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). He usually makes an interesting and constructive speech. He dealt at some length with the housing situation. I was rather intrigued with the novel proposal he made-and I say "novel" because it is new as far as the government or the members of this house are concerned -urging the government to establish some form of equity insurance for the down payment on homes. As I understood his remarks at the time-and since then I have read them carefully-his proposal would not cost this country one cent. It might mean certain careful administrative arrangements and some little extra work for the department concerned, but I completely agree with his analysis of the situation, with his proposals and with the benefit that would accrue to the home purchaser without any cost to
this country. I urge the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who is in charge of the housing act, to give serious consideration to this constructive and, in my opinion, forward-looking proposal.
I have come to the conclusion of my dealing with subjects that have been concerned with water and land. I now come to the air. For years I have been urging better facilities to improve radio reception in the northern half of my constituency, particularly. For years thousands of my constituents have not had the opportunity to listen to a Canadian radio station properly, and that situation exists at the present time. If they want to listen to a radio station satisfactorily, because of the mountainous terrain and unusual circumstances and the difficulties that prevail with regard to radio transmission they have had to satisfy themselves with listening to San Francisco, Seattle or some Central American station. Last year two low-power relay transmitters were established in my constituency, one at Castlegar, and one at Kaslo. I want to say that the people of the areas served by those low-power relay transmitters are delighted with their installation. For the first time in their experience as residents of Kootenay West they have had the opportunity to listen to the C.B.C. from seven o'clock in the morning until eleven o'clock at night, and they enjoy it greatly.
But their enjoyment has created a great deal of interest among those who are not now enjoying such radio reception. On December 20 last I addressed a meeting at which were present over 300 people from various points along the Arrow lakes, and they discussed this question. That meeting passed a resolution urging the government to take action to bring about the installation of low-power relay stations in Kootenay West sufficient to cover the balance of the district which is at present suffering from poor reception.
I urge the minister of the department concerned to give consideration to this appeal. While other people-and soon possibly the majority of the people in Canada-are enjoying television, I have thousands of residents in my constituency who have never had the opportunity, since radio was first instituted, to enjoy proper Canadian radio reception. I urge early action to correct this unnecessary and, in my opinion, most unfair situation.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity of again saying a word as the representative of one of the finest and most progressive ridings in Canada. That goes without question. Like other hon. members. I congratulate
262	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Mclvor and welcome the new members. I have personally congratulated the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should very much like to welcome the seven new members of the page staff. They are vital to the life of this house, and they are great boys.
There are some things that we miss on this side of the house. For one thing, we miss the clock. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) tells me that there is therefore no limit on the speakers on this side of the house; but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I shall not go my 40 minutes unless something happens that has not happened previously. I say with a good deal of feeling that, as I look across at his empty seat, I miss the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). I know the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) is doing a good job but, as I say, I miss the Leader of the Opposition. On former occasions he would sit through my speech for 30 minutes without batting an eye. Who would not appreciate that courtesy? We hope that soon, in answer to the quiet petitions of members of this house, the Leader of the Opposition will be restored to health and strength.
Having read and reread the speech from the throne, may I say that in my opinion it is the best that has been made in my short term in the house. I believe I have listened to 19 or 20 speeches from the throne. The present one deals with the general life of Canada better than any speech from the throne I have read. It is not in general but in particular language. After dealing first with certain outstanding questions it deals at the close of the speech with 15 pieces of legislation that will be dealt with by the house. Nobody speaking the truth dares to say that the speech from the throne is distinguished for what it does not say. It is distinguished for what it does say, and I think I can prove that.
The first thing in the speech from the throne that I appreciated was the fact that a committee of the house is to be set up to deal with the rules and procedure of the house. I do not think any man needs to speak for 40 minutes, because there are so many opportunities for members who wish to speak on the various questions that come before us. In the second place, if there is some matter that is burning our insides we can put a question about it and get the information. I think 40 minutes is too long. We will have to prepare more thoroughly. I know that those who speak loud and long and very intelligently may oppose cutting down the time, but I think their better judgment will lead them to see that this is a step in the right
IMr. Mclvor.]

direction. I am looking forward to the report of the committee with a great deal of interest.
The speech from the throne also indicates that the government is considering the needs of the blind. The age limit is to be cut to 18 years. However, when the matter comes before the house I am going to urge the house that the blind should get their pensions without a means test. Consider the man or woman who has to go through the world without sight. You cannot compensate them in any way. It is a terrible handicap.
The amendment of the Unemployment Insurance Act is most welcome because we believe it will do a good deal to help those who are not working. It tells me that the government is alive to the needs of the day, which are to keep men working or if they are not working to give them enough to live on so they will have the necessities of life and a little more.
In sport, Mr. Speaker, some athletes are honoured because they break records. It may be scoring a certain number of goals, it may be that a goalkeeper has so many shut-outs, it may be that a man has hit so many home runs or stolen so many bases. I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) has made a record in the House of Commons when he can bring in a money bill preceded by a resolution and in two days have it passed through the house and the other place. The bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced by way of resolution at 3 p.m. on Tuesday, January 11. The resolution was passed and the bill was given first reading on that day. Second reading of the bill was moved at 3.10 p.m. on Thursday, January 13. The bill received second reading, went through committee and by 5.15 p.m. was passed by the house. Before the day ended it was not only passed by the House of Commons but had been passed by the other place. All this was done in two days. We congratulate the minister on this record. It will be pretty hard for any other minister to beat it.
According to the speech from the throne the government is also going to deal with the needs of the veterans. Veterans allowances are going to be improved. For six years now I have been advocating that veterans of the first and second world wars, but particularly the first world war, should receive a pension at 60 years of age without a means test. I know some veterans in Fort William who are about 60 years old, and I can tell hon. members that they could not compete with me in athletic contests because they lost so much during those years of war. One man had four Christmas dinners in the trenches.
These men risked their lives. They left

everything that was near and dear. Some of them came back, and those who did not need no pension; they have heard their "well done". As long as I am here I am going to press for a pension at 60 without a means test for the veterans of these two wars.
We were also pleased to learn that the Colombo plan not only continues to be supported and kept going in the old way but is being strengthened by a grant of an additional million dollars. Some people believe this is not enough, but to me a million dollars is a lot of money. An additional million dollars will strengthen the Colombo plan.
We are also assured that pensions for the handicapped will be put into effect. This is what we expected. I know we fought for them for quite a while. I said in the house I would not support any other social legislation until pensions for the handicapped were granted. Now we can support other legislation along similar lines.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) congratulated the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) on the speech he made. I congratulate him too. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) knows the hon. member is right when he says that any man who invests $1,500 in a new house should not lose his investment because of adverse circumstances such as sickness or unemployment. I congratulate the hon. member for Spadina on his splendidly prepared speech and the clear and concise way in which he delivered it.
I know we too have a problem at Fort William in the form of unemployment. The local member of the legislature for Port Arthur, who is a Conservative but who speaks the truth because he is a sincere man and a real friend-

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) made a good speech. I like to hear him, because I believe he speaks sincerely. I do not say that no one else speaks sincerely, but I like to hear him. We not only think that ourselves, but there are those outside of Canada who congratulate Canada on its government. I should like to say there are those to the south of us who think we are doing a very good job. This summer the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was presented with the Guggenheim medal by the American Society of Engineers because of his aid to aviation. This is one of the highest tributes that could be paid to a minister.
When I think of Canada, there is music in the name. When I think of Canada from east to west, with all its provincial governments, its cities and its federal government, I am sure we have the best governments on earth. The opposition may talk as they like, but in their own hearts they know that we have good government. It is honest. I dare any man to stand up in this house or out of it and point a finger at a cabinet minister for taking one personal dollar of graft. After 20 years in office, Mr. Speaker, I feel that is a fine record. Where is there a provincial government that can match that record? speechtext:
I am not listening to interruptions. We have a great country. When I think of Fort William I think of what our city council is doing. As I have mentioned before, we are training our youth to become clean, Christian citizens. The city council is doing one job and our Sunday schools, churches and Y.M.C.A. are doing another. We have 29 hockey and skating rinks side by side. They are supervised by a superintendent who likes boys. There is a house at each rink. When I think of that, I admire our city council and its progress. The taxes in that city are no higher than in any other city. They are not even as high as in Ottawa.

The Address-Mr. Mclvor ' In the summertime we have our parks board manager, Mr. Art Widnall. He has high school pupils and others who supervise the children in the different parks during the summer, so the boys and girls are kept busy. One of the outstanding features is that we have so many hockey teams in these rinks it is difficult to get individuals to supervise them. I remember once asking a big fellow if he would come out and have a look at what we were doing. I announced there would be a practice for pee-wees, 12 years and under, on Thursday afternoon at 4.15. This was an open air rink, and it was 15 below with a wind blowing. This big fellow, Ted Grant, a city policeman, came along, but neither he nor anybody else was cold that afternoon. Today this big policeman is carrying on, and he will never have less than three teams to supervise. He supervises baseball during the summer, and the boys are not afraid of him. Of course, they will do what he says.
I heard the leader of the C.C.F. say that nothing had been done for the benefit of the workers from 1935 to 1938. I do not know what was done in Rosetown-Biggar, but I know what was done in Fort William and district. The then deputy minister of labour, and afterward the late Humphrey Mitchell, came out. The relief camps were closed and the men were put at emergency work for the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. That was a month after our election, and I appreciated that very much.
I should like to say a word about strikes. I have been hoping that the brains of labour, which I believe are just as good as any others, would co-operate with management in finding a cure for strikes. I know that industries in Canada are growing. When we suggest co-operation between labour and management and a share in the profits for the worker as a cure for strikes, we know that will not work in companies like the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. However, perhaps it could be worked out.
I am convinced that if you could give the worker his present salary plus a share in the profits that would work splendidly. Of course there are those who suggest that if you could get the golden rule put into practice it would cure strikes, and I am convinced that it would.
Fort William has some needs. In order to cure our unemployment we think we should have a breakwater in front of No. 2 and No. 1. It is needed for the storage of logs and the protection of industries. We know that the dominion government pays $33,000 for offices in Fort William, but we would like to have a federal building. We strongly advocate that dredging should be begun as


early as possible instead of at the beginning of July. We think dredging should be started early in the spring.
I was told by a friend that Canada's danger today is not communism and is not war. I said, "Well, what is it?" He said it .is the breaking of the ten commandments. I have thought a good deal about it. I have heard hon. members in this house debate the question of divorce, but I have not yet heard anyone give us a cure for divorce. The cause of divorce is the breaking of the seventh commandment; therefore my friend was right in saying the danger to Canada was the breaking of the ten commandments. The number of divorces is increasing every year. Why? Because of selfishness and the breaking of the seventh commandment.
I was in British Columbia this fall. I know that a man who visits another province and expects to assess the life in that province in a week is expecting a great deal. I could not do it. When I went to Vancouver I did find that there was a big ruction because certain individuals were putting out sweepstake tickets with promises of big rewards. A certain newspaper and the police checked up and found that no one had ever received a prize.
The cry all across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific is, "Buy a sweepstake ticket and get something for nothing." What commandment does that break? The tenth commandment says "Thou shalt not covet." He is just trying to get something the other fellow has paid for. Therefore the danger to Canada today is in the breaking of the ten commandments.
What do we find today in respect to working conditions? In the past we struggled hard for one day in seven for the workingman. He got one day in seven; now he has two. Some think it should be cut down a little lower, but I do not. We have the eight-hour day and the five-day week, therefore there are eight hours for work, eight hours for play and eight hours for sleep, with a full day on Saturday. Yet you find those who want to steal Sunday from the Almighty and make it a day of commercial sport. That is unpopular, and it is an unpopular thing to advocate. It is as true as life that when you hold your commercial activities on the Sabbath day, you are breaking a moral law, "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy."
I am not going to push that any farther, but I should like to add that this friend pf mine says, "You have departments for war; why not have a department for peace?" With respect to the breaking of the Sabbath day,

I would advise cabinet ministers whose officials put on displays on the Sabbath, that many young men and maidens are leading children to Sunday school on the Sabbath day. I would ask them to refrain from putting on any exhibitions on the Sabbath day because you, Mr. Speaker, in leading us in prayer will recall that one petition in it is, "Lead us not into temptation." A big display by any department of government on the Sabbath day does lead children and older people away. Therefore I would say to them, "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy."
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your patience. There is one thing troubling me at the present time. The constituents of Fort William have treated me beyond any expectation I ever had. In fact I had a group call on me the other day. They do not think as I do, but they told me that I represented everybody in the constituency. I said, "No, I do not" and I knew whom I was talking to. I do not represent those who treat God as a myth or represent anything that that represents. I do not represent them and I do not claim to represent them, but of course I might try to change their minds. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions it has been my privilege either to follow or precede the hon. member for Fort William, and I am happy to say that on many of these occasions we have been able to see eye to eye on a good many questions. Tonight, as I had the privilege of again listening to him, I could agree heartily with many of the things he said.
The hon. member for Fort William spent some time out in the area that I have the privilege of representing, the Brandon-Souris constituency, and he left his mark there so far as spiritual values are concerned. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member will pardon me if I cannot agree with him in all things he has said with respect to the government and government policies, and I crave his indulgence in that regard.
As is usual in the throne speech debate, hon. members supporting the government spend a great deal of time extolling the virtues of the present administration. However, during this debate I detect an almost forced attempt to support the policies of the government, as revealed by the speech from the throne. Indeed it is almost possible to conclude that "they protest too much".
The throne speech, as I analyse it, assumes a cautious tone for the first time during 50433-18
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale my short experience in the house. I remember the first throne speech it was my privilege to listen to back in 1951. It was almost as buoyant in its tone as the inflation it was attempting to deal with at that time. There is one conclusion we can reach thus far in the discussion, namely that Canada is passing through a period of transition at the present moment.
In his recent speech the president of the Bank of Montreal suggested that we were in a phase of economic development where it was impossible to conclude whether Canada was heading into a period of deflation or inflation. When I read that statement it occurred to me that it might account for the early retirement of the highly respected governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers, who at a comparatively youthful age, in his early fifties, has decided to relinquish that important post. It may be that resting on the horns of this insoluble dilemma, trying to decide whether we are heading toward deflation or inflation, has necessitated this unfortunate early retirement, because nothing is more exhausting to the nervous as well as to the physical energy than to be faced with an insoluble dilemma of that kind.
I would like to say one other thing in a general way about the speech from the throne. I must say this much for it. At least it deals with the problems confronting Canada at the present time in the correct order of emphasis. It places international affairs first. It refers to the continuing threat of war in the atomic age, and it also has an optimistic reference to the continuing cold war. I am not going to deal further with that aspect of the throne speech at the moment; there will be an opportunity later this week. It also mentions the Colombo plan, and in passing I should like to express disappointment at the small increase that is to be forthcoming for that very important activity in the sphere of international affairs.
The next matter dealt with was internal welfare. I join with other hon. members in expressing pleasure at the adoption of the disability pension plan for Canada, a plan pioneered by the Ontario Conservative government. The same applies to the other welfare measures, the pension for the blind and the war veterans allowance. In passing I urge that attention be paid to the last section of the amendment of this group to the effect that a contributory health insurance program be implemented at the earliest possible moment. It is one of the great gaps in the system of social security in our dominion at the present time.
