The Address

Mr. Dinsdale
Those remarks made in passing deal in a general way with the speech from the throne to which we listened just over a week ago. As I have already indicated, we can all agree -and the opinion has been expressed from all sides of the house-that Canada is passing through a period of rather uncertain economic transition.
I have before me many economic reviews from government departments and commercial and banking institutions, all of which point in this same direction. In fact there are so many statistics available today to the ordinary private member of this house that it is very difficult to gather any rhyme or reason from them. Speakers and documents, I sometimes feel, spout statistics like a demented quarterback, and it becomes very difficult for the ordinary member to make an adequate appraisal of the situation. I have here, however, a good summation which I found in a Bank of Montreal Review of June 24, 1954:
It is now clear that after climbing persistently and often rapidly since 1946 business activity reached a peak in the autumn of 1953 and entered upon a gentle downward slope, the contours of which are still being mapped.
I think that is a good summary of the economic situation facing us at the moment. As has already been indicated, supporters of the government would perhaps deny that appraisal and would tend to emphasize the rosier aspect of the picture. On the other hand supporters of the group to my left, the C.C.F., would see in this transition another case of heading for a major depression which has been an unfortunate peculiarity of our so-called capitalistic system, at least since the beginning of the industrial revolution.
Despite the fact that the government backbenchers try to present the rosier aspects, some of the measures presented by the government indicate at least a vague awareness of the problems. The fact that we suspended the debate on the speech from the throne in order to pass some amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act is indicative of this.
Considerable anxiety is also being expressed concerning the trade difficulties confronting Canada at the present time. Europe has recovered in a spectacular way during the past year. Whereas in previous years the economic summaries of the outstanding financial and economic journals have been pointing to the rapid upsurge in the Canadian economy, the picture now is different and we find the same journals pointing to the remarkable recovery of the European economy. Because of her dependence on export trade Canada is placed in a very embarrassing position as the result. This was


highlighted to me as I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in his rebuttal to the speech of the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) on Monday last. During the course of that speech the Prime Minister picked upon what he thought was an indirect reference to protectionism, or what is very often referred to in this house as a policy of Tory protectionism.
Reference has also been made from time to time to a famous speech made back in the thirties when Canada was in the throes of a world-wide depression. The prime minister of that day in trying to cope with the very disastrous trade situation confronting Canada as a result of the world-wide depression indicated that he was going to blast his way into the markets of the world. I have been very intrigued and interested by the fact that almost invariably when we get on to the theme of trade in this house, some hon. member on the other side refers to that particular quotation.
I would like to say that a legitimate and enthusiastic attempt to restore Canada's trade position, or if you prefer to use the phrase "blast our way into the markets of the world", is much more effective than the blasting process referred to in the speech from the throne-the blasting of Ripple Rock. As far as I am concerned it has no connection at all with the trade situation confronting us.
We are all disturbed and distressed, particularly those of us from the prairies, the continental west, at the obstacles which are confronting GATT at the present time. As I understand it, when GATT was formulated it was the hope that it would lead inevitably to an international trade association, just as during those halcyon days it was the hope that the United Nations would lead the world into a period of blissful peace and contentment, ad infinitum.
I understand that at the time GATT was being negotiated all sides of the house were very strongly and enthusiastically in support of the trade policies represented therein. Unfortunately, the best laid plans of mice and men "gang aft agley". In our attempts to establish a system of international security we are faced with similar difficulties in the realm of trade as in the realm of military defence. Economic nationalism is just as difficult to deal with as is military nationalism, and economic warfare is just as real as is the other type of warfare that constantly threatens the world at the present time.
When we consider that the country closest to us, the country toward which we have
JANUARY 17, 1955 moved as a market for our exports, the United States, has been making threatening gestures in reference to certain of our agricultural products, I think it will be readily appreciated how much more difficult the problem is when we are dealing with countries that are not in the least friendly toward us.
I might go even further on this question of economic nationalism. We are at least able to negotiate with the U.S.S.R. in regard to international security, but we cannot even get into communication with them, it would seem, with reference to this economic warfare with which we are faced.
I think we can conclude that there is a vast difference between theory and practice as far as economic disarmament is concerned. It is just as difficult, or perhaps even more so, as is the achieving of military disarmament. The experience of this country has been such as to make that almost axiomatic.
So far as the west is concerned, this problem affects us very intimately indeed. It particularly affects the three prairie provinces, whose economy is still based on the wheat trade. Wheat is still the economic lodestar of the prairies. I believe that when Sir Wilfrid Laurier prophesied at the beginning of the century that the twentieth century would belong to Canada, he had in mind the rapid development of the wheat trade on the prairies. Wheat made possible the building of Canada's first transcontinental railway, and I sometimes think the construction of the C.P.R. was the last major effort on the part of this dominion government relative to the prairies. It was conceived early in the history of this country and carried out with a magnificent vision that has since been justified many times over, even though there were many pessimists at that time.
I think it is also necessary to emphasize that the present request for some relief on the Crowsnest pass rate should take into consideration the contribution the wheat industry has made to the development of the railway system throughout Canada. It was also the rapid development of our wheat economy that made possible the great waves of immigration in the early years of this century and opened up that part of Canada to popular settlement. Unfortunately that trend has not continued with the same degree of rapidity, for reasons I shall deal with before I conclude my remarks.
Important as the wheat trade undoubtedly is, it nevertheless leaves our prairie economy in a particularly vulnerable position because it means we are tied to a one-product
50433-18J
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale economy. When disturbances inevitably occur in world economy and are reflected in our internal economy, it is the agricultural industry that is first to suffer. You cannot have a healthy economic situation while you have an immature economy, and the prairie economy will always remain immature while it is dependent on one product. The wheat trade, regardless of changing prices and changing economic circumstances, except under extreme conditions such as those produced by world wars is subjected to comparatively inflexible conditions. This point was brought out by Professor Alfred Marshall in his "Industry and Trade" published in 1919, when he said:
An exceptional "principle" applies to staple grain: because a fall in prices cannot generally increase its consumption as human food; and when it becomes dear, people will still buy enough of it to keep alive so long as they have means of purchase; in modern phraseology the demand for it is exceptionally inelastic.
That increases the difficulty of our prairie economy, and we have been continually subjected to boom and bust cycles which in more recent years have led to demands for methods of marketing that will take some of the sting out of the fluctuating trade cycle.
In this regard I would like to add, Mr. Speaker, that the wheat board has been particularly effective in smoothing out extreme swings in the economic cycle. The only difficulty with the wheat board is that it has tended to become used as an instrument of political manipulation, and wheat policies have been adapted to the welfare of the party in power. This, I feel, occurred quite recently in connection with the by-election in the constituency of Selkirk. An important announcement concerning interim payments was made the Saturday before voting took place. Other examples of this kind could be given.
With the spectre of a wheat problem hovering over the world once more, drastic action has to be taken in order to preserve our agricultural industry. Admittedly we are much better off now than we were in the thirties when the wheat surplus of that period unfortunately coincided with the market crash of 1929, and the whole wheat economy collapsed completely not only on the prairies but throughout the world. However,
I believe there need be no repetition of this disastrous episode, because our appreciation of this problem is much keener now than hitherto.
Some claim that the party to which I belong is not too concerned with the attitude of the government toward these economic problems. For my own part I believe that
268	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale government inactivity is in some cases almost as bad as too much government interference, and I believe there has not been a keen enough appreciation of the situation confronting the agricultural west at the present time.
Many hon. members who have already spoken in this debate have submitted ideas the acceptance and implementation of which might further stabilize the situation. For example, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) mentioned five points the other day. He suggested a 95 per cent parity forward pricing system; and that, of course, springs from the fact that agriculture is facing an increasing price squeeze at the present time. We have a support price system now, and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggested that it be used much more vigorously than it has been hitherto. I agree with him on that score. I believe, however, that if we fixed parity at a 95 per cent level we would be aggravating rather than solving the problem, because it would introduce further rigidity into our economic system. When the United States are moving away from a high level parity I believe it would be unfortunate if we tried to occupy a position they are now abandoning.
The hon. member suggested marketing boards, and this also is being adopted in agricultural circles as a method whereby the boom-bust cycle to which I referred, and its inherent fluctuations, can be stabilized. I would add, though, that marketing boards do not necessarily increase the price to the producer. They merely iron out some of the wilder fluctuations. In the final analysis it is demand that determines price. Relative to any increase in the number of marketing boards, it should be emphasized that the producers should themselves organize and obtain control of such boards. Nothing would be worse than to have marketing boards used as political instruments in the hands of any particular party in power.
The two-price system was mentioned, which involves dumping our agricultural products on the external market and maintaining the domestic price at a higher level. In that regard I think it almost inevitable that we would be faced with a tariff war such as that which occurred in the 1930's. If we started dumping our agricultural products into the European market, or into any other market for that matter, they would retaliate with tariffs as they did in the 1930's. We must remember constantly that we have that problem of economic warfare, and that we are not all one big happy family in the world as yet.


I was reading in a review called "Crisis in Wheat, 1926-1954" some extremely interesting information concerning the tariff policy of certain European countries in the 1930's.
France began early to put duties on wheat imports. But as the wheat crisis deepened this process was speeded up and intensified as shown by the rates of duty prevailing in the following years. The rates are expressed in francs per quintal of grain.
The rates were as follows:	In 1921, 7
francs; in 1926, 18 francs; in 1929, 50 francs; and in 1936, 83 francs, equivalent to $1.50 a bushel. I was quite amazed too, to see the German reaction and the way they had pushed up the tariff. In 1930 the duty stood at 35 reichsmarks per quintal, which was about the equivalent of $3.84 a bushel. No wonder the prime minister of that time talked about blasting his way into the markets of the world, when he had to face tariff barriers of that kind. Even though we have moved along in our international thinking, I do not think we can expect the European market to acquiesce in a dumping policy on the part of the Canadian agriculture industry. Such a policy could only result in retaliatory tariffs.
The fifth point was the suggestion that we could investigate the price spread. This is a question that comes up repeatedly, and I have not time to harp on it at the moment. In the Virden Empire-Advance for February 10, 1954, I notice an article by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who has the responsibility for combines investigation. He had apparently been subjected to some inquiries concerning this spread, particularly in reference to meat prices, between the price received by the producer and the price paid by the consumer. He had a long article trying to explain why this situation occurs. Then he said:
Let me say, as the minister responsible for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. that all complaints of this nature regarding the suspected existence of any such combine are thoroughly investigated. So if you have any yourself or know of any friends who have complaints of this sort to make, do not hesitate to bring them to our attention.
I have accepted that invitation tonight, and I am agreeing with the hon. member for Dauphin that there might be an extremely fruitful field for investigation in this regard. I am sorry that time does not permit my further development of that question.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had some recommendations to make with regard to agriculture. He suggested that something be done about the cash situation among the farmers. The city of Brandon that I represent is most directly affected by the cash shortage because we are

largely a city serving the surrounding agricultural area. I made a survey in recent months among the retail merchants, and they are not at all happy about the situation. Something must be done in order to place cash into the hands of the grain farmers. During these periods of economic transition, unfortunately the credit facilities extended to other business activities in Canada do not apply top directly to the agricultural economy.
In the first instance the farmer is rather suspicious of debt, mainly because of his unfortunate experience during the 1930's and during the earlier periods of the boom-and-bust cycle. Then I came up against a special problem of this kind during the past summer when we had flooding on the Assiniboine river. That flooding has occurred twice in succession now, and there were groups of farmers who had had a complete crop failure for two years in succession. It is bad enough to take one crop failure, but it creates an almost hopeless economic situation to take two. There is no solution to their immediate financial problem. As is well known, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act does not cover that situation. There they were, left to sink or to swim according to their own ability. That is a situation that could well bear investigation by the government.
I agree heartily with the hon. member for Prince Albert that we could be more aggressive in our marketing policy. We have tended to become a bit slothful and soft in recent years because of the overwhelming demand from the foreign market. We might well do a little bit of "blasting", if I might use that word in quotation marks, in order to ease the present situation. Of course I most heartily agree with the extension of customs facilities at port Churchill, because we on the prairies believe that port Churchill has a great future as a port providing access to the European market.
To sum all this up, Mr. Speaker, agriculture is operating within a highly complex industrial society in which free enterprise is drastically modified by tariffs, fiscal policy, monopolies and so forth, largely because we are confronted with an unpredictable, uncontrolled external situation. I believe that there are some measures this government can take without resorting to tariffs-that nasty word -controls and so forth, which only tend to increase economic rigidity.
In the time remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that what we should do is take into consideration the nature of Canada's present boom. We have been enjoying a boom since 1946 up until recent months. As I have already emphasized and now re-emphasize,
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale this boom is a boom without a bust. As to business cycles, the bugbear of our capitalistic system, it is felt by economic authorities that we have at last beaten this bugaboo, this bugbear, and that we are now in a position to handle or iron out the harsher aspects of the boom-bust cycle.
The present boom in Canada's economy, as I see it, has two prongs; first, that in the primary resources industry and second, that in manufacturing. This primary resources boom is something new to our Canadian economy; and it is this primary resources boom that is giving the little shot in the arm that we have in the west at the present time and also in the northern regions. In many aspects, as a result of the boom in primary resources the north is becoming what the west was to Canada some 80 years ago.
The discovery of these resources is not necessarily new. We have known of their existence for some time. It has only become possible during recent years, particularly during and since the war, for Canada to exploit these resources because of the efforts of geologists and bush pilots. This being so, I was amazed last year when the government refused to grant a charter to Canadian Pacific: Air Lines, which had requested the privilege of providing a cheap freight service in the northern part of Canada. I have before me a newspaper clipping which impresses me as being somewhat of an obituary in this regard. The heading of the article is "Canadian Pacific Air Lines Sells Two Giant Planes". It sold two DC-6A planes that it had purchased in anticipation that a forwardlooking government would welcome an increase in freight transportation facilities in the rapidly developing northland. It is hard for me to understand the negative policy of the government in this regard.
I have had some personal contact with the boom in resources, because right in the middle of my constituency is Virden, which has become the oil centre of Manitoba. Just out of curiosity I took a recent edition of the Virden Empire-Advance and clipped four different articles dealing with the oil boom in that part of the province. The first article is headed, "Manitoba on the March". The next article is headed, "Twenty-six New Oil Wells Spur November Production". The next one is "Manitoba Steps Into Ranks of Major Areas of Canadian Oil Development." Indeed, we have moved forward so rapidly that Manitoba hopes to be self-sufficient in oil in a very short time.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) is aware of the fact that Virden is a boom town, because I think he has been besieged

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale recently by protests concerning the inadequacy of the post office facilities in that community. The town has grown so quickly and subscribers have increased so rapidly that the post office service has become somewhat outmoded. I believe the Postmaster General is wrestling with that difficulty at the moment; at least I trust that he is.
This is all well and good as far as primary resources are concerned, but it is in the area of manufacturing that the west is weakest. We lack secondary industry. The great boom in manufacturing has all been concentrated around Montreal and Toronto. In other words the geographic pattern of industrial and manufacturing activity still remains much the same as it has been during the whole long stretch of the first half of the twentieth century. The shift to the west so far as economic change is concerned is merely a movement of ideas and money rather than manufacturing production. The brains and capital required in the search for primary products are largely being found in the eastern part of the country. I must add that the men with those brains came from the west to be trained in the universities of the east, and are now finding their way back to the prairies again. One of our chief exports from the prairies has always been men of outstanding ability.
In addition to that concentration in eastern Canada, there is the same concentration in the United States. In fact it may be said that to a great extent Canada's boom is based on and spearheaded by the relative United States boom. We have played into their hands with reference to trade. As has been pointed out by many speakers, United States capital invested in Canada now amounts to $7,235 million, $3 billion of which represents investments in companies actually controlled in the United States. As a result there has been a relative dropping off in our exports to Britain.
I think it should be noted, too, that United States capital has largely developed the Lynn Lake area in Manitoba, the oil industry, and Kitimat in British Columbia. I do not decry that fact. It is necessary at the present stage of development. I am merely pointing out that it does not help solve the problem of the prairies. That problem can only be solved if together with the boom in resources expansion and development we have an equivalent development in the secondary or manufacturing industries. If that does not happen our second state is going to be worse than the first, because if we have a sudden vacuum created in the western region after the initial exploration is over, a vacuum that


has not been filled by secondary industrial activity, we are going to be badly off indeed.
I sometimes feel, Mr. Speaker, that the national policy that was so successfully pushed forward by the first administration of this country stopped short at the head of the lakes, and nothing has been done to develop a mature economy on the prairies. Because of all this and much more that I could say if time permitted, I subscribe heartily to the amendment moved by the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe), particularly paragraph (e) thereof, which reads as follows:
to facilitate and encourage the processing of our natural resources in Canada, and thereby increase opportunities and employment for Canadians.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, words fail to adequately express my dissatisfaction with the government for failing to deal with a very important aspect of the Canadian economy in the speech from the throne. I noted that the speech mentioned the great disasters that had befallen Nova Scotia and Ontario, and I was pleased to note that certain measures were outlined offering some relief to those stricken areas. But, Mr. Speaker, no mention was made of the disaster that struck western Canada this year. Rust in western Canada wrought a havoc that was worse in many respects than the drought of 1937. Some areas had a lower yield than in the worst years of the drought period.
The speech from the throne also says that the relatively poor wheat crop is being reflected by a small decline in the total national income. The only concern the Liberal government of today has with the west is that the west was inconsiderate enough to have a bad crop which will be reflected in a decline in the total national income. No mention was made of offering some measure of relief by amending the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to bring it in line with the present cost of production. Under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act the maximum amount a farmer may receive is $500 if he lives in a township in which the average yield of wheat is not more than four bushels per acre. This legislation was passed many years ago when the cost of farm production was but a fraction of what it is today. It seems to me that the farmers are justified in demanding revision of the act to bring it up to date.
Tied in with that, Mr. Speaker, there is the almost forgotten paragraph in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which states that if the average yield is between 8 and 12 bushels of wheat per acre, and if the average price of

The Address-Mr. W. M. Johnson
wheat should fall below a certain level, compensation will be paid. This is in paragraph (a) of subsection 2 of section 3. The only trouble is that it specifies that if the price of wheat should fall below 80 cents per bushel, then payment will be made. There again, Mr. Speaker, this price was set in 1939. When we consider the devaluation of our dollar, in effect the farmer who is producing feed wheat is receiving in the neighbourhood of 40 cents a bushel.
Yes, the Liberal government today is trying to get itself off the hook by saying it is the poor crop in western Canada that is creating these conditions. No, Mr. Speaker, it is the same factor that has created these conditions and that has brought about a marked increase in unemployment; it is not the poor crop but just plain, ordinary poor government.
The cash farm income for the first nine months of this year is less than half that of the previous year. There is a drop of $217 million, and the net income in Canada continues the decline it started three years ago. I feel we should give some consideration, not to whether this poor crop affects the national income but how this poor crop affects the livelihood of the farmers. It is not the poor crop that has given us these conditions in western Canada, because I do not know of a single farmer who has been unable to fill his quota. With only a poor crop he would not have had the grain to fill his quota, so there must be other factors to consider. The fact is that in the first five months of the crop year wheat deliveries from the farms in the prairie provinces were the lowest in the entire history of the present Canadian wheat board.
The estimates for the first five months of this year show that farmers have delivered 107 million bushels. The ten-year average is 211 million bushels, or 104 million bushels greater. Last year we thought things were bad enough when deliveries in this period were 228 million bushels. At the start of this year nearly three-quarters of the marketing points in western Canada were on a two-bushel quota. This meant that in this crop year the farmers were unable to deliver more than two bushels per specified acre.
The serious aspect of this, Mr. Speaker, was that in many of these marketing points the quota was not granted until the early part or middle of December. This meant that the farmer operated from the end of the last crop year up to the middle of December without receiving one cent in cash from that crop.	[DOT]
In western Canada there were two consequences of the rust. First of all it lowered
the yield, and secondly it raised havoc with the grades. It meant that the farmer who had low grade or feed wheat, for example, got 87-5 cents per bushel and was only able to market two bushels per acre. This will give you some idea of the money he has had to work with over the past few months.
In view of the conditions that existed, it certainly should not have taken a political event such as the Selkirk by-election to bring about the announcement of an interim payment of 10 cents a bushel. This announcement was made in October, and all cheques were to be in the mail by December 21. By December 21 the farmers had been able, in many instances, to deliver some grain. The interim payment should have been made when farmers really needed it, in September and early October. Further, there should be an immediate announcement of another interim payment of 10 cents a bushel, with the final payment on last year's crop being made in the spring.
While I am discussing an agricultural problem such as grain, I do not think I can completely cover it without some mention of this matter of box car allocation. Last year the agriculture and colonization committee thoroughly discussed the problem. It was proved to the satisfaction of many members of that committee that the farmers and farm organizations were 100 per cent behind some equitable system. We even received assurance from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that something was going to be done about it. When I returned this session, I was delighted to see on the order paper a resolution to amend the Canada Grain Act. I thought that finally the government was going to introduce some measure for the distribution of box cars that would enable the farmers to deliver their grain to the elevator for which they had a preference. I was pleased to think that the minister was carrying out the commitment he had made, and that something was going to be done about it.
Well, perhaps this is done as well as the Liberal government can do anything. Instead of amending the Canada Grain Act to provide for this system of box car allocation, what did they do? They provided for the appointment of four instead of three commissioners and raised the salary of the chief commissioner from $14,000 to $15,000 and that of the other two members from $12,000 to $13,500. Certainly that is a fine way to help this box car allocation.
I believe a lot of the blame in connection with this matter should rest with the government representatives from Saskatchewan. As a member of the agriculture and colonization

The Address-Mr. W. M. Johnson committee I was greatly disappointed to find that, although they represented western Canada, they were fighting vigorously against the interests of western Canada. I do not see how they could go back to meet the wheat pool organizations, attend the wheat pool annual meetings and farmers' meetings, knowing they had failed to fight for some amendment to the Canada Grain Act to make provision for this important matter.
Time is running out. The period of congestion is still with us. We have nearly 900 million bushels of wheat in storage, but we have had a very light crop in western Canada, estimated at 300 million bushels. This may mean that the problem of box car allocation may not be as important in the future as it has been in the past.
This government has failed to grant this concession to the farmers of western Canada. Perhaps it was not the failure of the government. Perhaps it is the only thing we can expect of a government that is dedicated to following the principles of capitalism and profit, to accede to the wishes of the large privately-owned grain companies.
This has dealt a blow to the co-operative grain handling movement that will be felt for many years to come. Just before I leave this subject of box car allocation, some claim that we should lay some blame on the shoulders of the top officials of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I have heard some pool members say that these officials have not pursued this matter, which is of the utmost importance to the average member of the pool organization, with the same determination and vigour with which they fought some of the battles in the past. There may be hidden reasons for this action; there may be some reasons I may not be aware of, but it does seem to me that they are not putting up the battle on behalf of the membership of these great farm organizations that they did in past years.
Before leaving the matter of the Canada Grain Aot I should like to point out that the government promised to bring this matter before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for review. This promise was made two years ago, and I should like to see the government fulfil one of its promises. Perhaps it, too, is like the national health insurance promise and the act will not be reviewed in my lifetime.
In his address the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) dealt with another problem of the agricultural economy of Canada, namely the lack of consideration by the government in offering some measure of stabilization for farmers. No section of our economy is more subject to ups and downs

than those involved in agriculture. A man who raises cattle may spend a lot of money to get his herd built up and then find, when he gets into a position to recover something from his many years of work, that the bottom has dropped out of the market.
The same thing is true of the poultry and hog producers. I am always amazed when I hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) tell us that we have a floor price of 38 cents a dozen under eggs, implying that the farmers of Canada get 38 cents a dozen for their eggs. The floor price operates at the packer level, and the packing companies can pay just about any price they like to the farmers for their eggs, not only just the farmers of Saskatchewan but all the farmers of Canada.
So the sooner we can consolidate these problems and smooth out some of the difficulties that are facing this important segment of our economy, the sooner we can expect those other segments of the economy that are so dependent on agriculture to become completely healthy. When the farm economy suffers a decline, it is only a matter of a few years until the rest of the economy suffers a decline. We can see that by looking at past statistics. It is desirable, Mr. Speaker, before it is too late, that this government throw off some of its lethargy and start to give serious consideration to a pricing policy for agriculture-and I am speaking of all agriculture. I am speaking of the milk producers of Ontario and Quebec, the fruit growers of the east and the west, all segments of our agricultural economy, so that farmers' incomes can be levelled off and we shall get away from these ups and downs that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale) was just discussing.
As long as we are operating under the system of so-called free enterprise which the Liberal government and the Tories and the socreds claim to be following, it is inevitable that we shall have these booms and busts. It is one of the characteristics of the so-called capitalistic system, where the individuals look after themselves and show no concern for others in the economy. It is only when we can incorporate some Christian principles into our economic socialism that we can give a degree of relief to all of the people of Canada. Only when we forget about this profit motive, which has been leading us down the garden path, and resort to a little bit of common-sense planning, the same sense we use in our households and our own businesses; only by following some of these examples shall we level out these horrible ups and downs in our economy. Then in time we shall make this country of

ours the best place on earth to live in, a place where we can be proud to look forward to the future and a peaceful heritage, where we shall be granted some return for the efforts we put forth.

He said he spent a fair amount of time in the province of Quebec. I wonder on what day it was that he spent the fair amount of time in the province of Quebec. He referred to that great province as a sore spot in the matter of Canadian unity.
The Address-Mr. Proudfoot Might I point out that much could be learned about unity in the rest of Canada by looking at Quebec and what is done there. It has been my privilege to represent the constituency of Pontiac-Timiskaming in this house since 1949. I am proud of that constituency; I am also proud of the province in which I was born. I am proud of that constituency where my father was born, the same constituency where my grandfather was born and where my great-grandfather lived for 40 years.
I want to point out that the minorities have been fairly treated in the province of Quebec. Most certainly that is so when compared with the treatment of minorities in some other provinces of Canada. I would say that in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, 75 per cent of the people are of a different religious faith from myself, and at least 65 per cent of the people in that constituency are of French-Canadian origin. In the last two general elections, the voters of my constituency were willing to and did support me, and I believe those who opposed me did so not because I was of a racial religious minority group but rather because I happened to be of a different political faith.
At this time I would ask, could a man or woman of French-Canadian origin and Roman Catholic faith be elected in the riding of Burnaby-Coquitlam where, unfortunately, the majority of electors appear to be supporters of the socialist party? Will the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, who prates so much about national unity and talks in such a disparaging manner of the province of Quebec, indicate to me where in British Columbia, or indeed in any of the provinces outside of Quebec, racial majorities give evidence of similar generosity?
Then he goes on with his attack on Quebec because we do not see fit to have divorce courts in our province. I might add that neither has the province of Newfoundland. The subject of divorce courts in our province is a difficult and a delicate one, but surely the situation is not helped by a socialist proposition that it is proper to ram down the throats of the people of Quebec the suggestion that they must establish divorce courts whether they want them or not. Surely national unity involves the right of a substantial minority to oppose a measure that is offensive to them. Surely having a strong emphasis on family life and an abhorrence of divorce is not something to be condemned.
The hon. member refers to Quebec as a sore spot in Canadian unity because of some difficulty in a tax situation, but when you analyse his remarks his real criticism of the people of Quebec and of this government

The Address-Mr. Proudfoot seems to be because of the fact that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) accepted a request of the premier of Quebec to meet in Montreal to discuss this difficult problem of taxation rights as between the province of Quebec and the federal government. Surely the socialist party did not think the Prime Minister of Canada should miss an opportunity of settling this important taxation difficulty merely because of false pride or some mistaken consideration of dignity. Did not Churchill come to Ottawa? Did not Truman come to Ottawa? Did not our Prime Minister visit many countries on the greatest good-will tour ever made by a Canadian prime minister?
The men and women of Canada will applaud the Prime Minister for being a big enough man to seize the opportunity of dealing with a difficult problem. His action in going to Montreal was the action of a statesman. It is what all Canadians would have their prime minister do in the circumstances. It does not warrant the socialist member's reference to the province of Quebec as a sore spot in the matter of Canadian unity. That the hon. member does hold it against the province of Quebec is indicated in the following statement of his, which I quote:
In the city of Montreal the communist party polled about as many votes as the C.C.F.
All this indicates is that the people of Quebec reject the soul-destroying doctrines of socialism, and that they have no confidence in either branch of the socialist party.
The hon. member goes on to say that the people of Quebec are suffering, and that they are not enjoying the facilities in the field of education which they would like to enjoy. Does the hon. member not know that the minority group in Quebec have been granted and allowed to freely exercise all the rights and privileges which they require or desire in order to bring up their children in the beliefs of their parents? I venture to assert that Quebec is the only province where the rights of minorities are so fully protected in the field of education.
Why does not the hon. member take time off to compare the rights of minority groups in his province of British Columbia with those in Quebec. At this time I have in mind a place called Maillardville, British Columbia, and if I am not wrong I think possibly Maillardville is in the constituency of Burnaby-Coquitlam. I would ask him to examine the school laws of his province before he launches an attack on my province, and before he presumes to give advice to the people of Canada.
The hon. member says that his socialist party is the only party which has arisen out

of the needs of the people of Canada; but an examination of his speech indicates that his socialist party is rather seeking to arise out of the stirring up of prejudice and hatred in this country. Let me assure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and let me assure the people of Canada, that political tactics of the kind exemplified in his speech will not work in Quebec. I assure you the people of the province of Quebec know better.

The Right Honourable Louis S. St-Laurent, P.C., Q.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
Pursuant to our interview in Montreal on October 5th last and to the letter I sent you on the 11th of the same month, I am writing you on the subject of the provincial income tax in and for the province of Quebec.
We believe that we clearly defined the opinion arid the attitude of the government of the province of Quebec, in matters of the powers of taxation during the Canadian intergovernmental conferences which were held in Ottawa since 1945 and came to a close at Quebec in 1950, as well as in the correspondence we have had with federal authorities, particularly since 1949.
The agreement concluded between the preceding provincial government and the federal authorities, concerning important provincial powers of taxation, expired in 1947. Since then, the province of Quebec has not availed itself of its right to collect a provincial income tax in the province. This shows the earnest desire of the Quebec government to come to an agreement with Ottawa and, after all, the federal government has profited financially, to a large extent, by this situation which lasted approximately seven years.
The great progress and the tremendous developments, from which our immense province benefits, particularly large and

Federal-Provincial Fiscal Relations numerous districts which were formerly less-favoured, necessitate numerous public services and many improvements in several important fields of provincial administration, especially in the vital fields of education and hospitalization.
Such tremendous progress and the brilliant prospects before the province require a more complete utilization of the sources of provincial revenue. It is unnecessary to emphasize that the progress and prosperity of the province of Quebec make a truly worthy contribution to the progress and prosperity of the country in general.
Therefore, the Quebec legislature decided to levy, within the province, a provincial tax on personal income. Unquestionably, as agreed by all, it is a tax that the Canadian constitution authorizes Quebec to impose. Actually, this tax represents only approximately 10 per cent of the federal tax on personal income collected in the province of Quebec, because, even though our provincial tax is apparently calculated to be 15 per cent of the federal tax, the exemptions provided by the provincial law materially reduce this proportion.
In short, the provincial tax represents approximately 10 per cent of the federal income tax collected from the taxpayers in the province of Quebec and, by deducting the provincial tax from the federal tax, Ottawa will in fact receive about 90 per cent of the tax on personal income collected in the province of Quebec.
The federal authorities assert that the province and the federal government have concurrent rights of taxing personal income. About 10 per cent to the province and about 90 per cent to Ottawa is an extraordinarily reasonable concurrence, you will no doubt agree. Furthermore, it should be recalled that our provincial income tax is used entirely for purposes of education and hospitalization, public health and social legislation among others, in and for the province.
Since the end of the last war-I merely mention facts without details or appraisal- some provinces have abandoned to the central authority certain important sources of provincial income in return for payment by Ottawa of federal subsidies to these provinces.
We have said on several occasions that the province of Quebec wishes to retain its powers of taxation and does not wish to exchange them for subsidies. We consider it our duty to maintain such an attitude.
We are ready to enter into a really temporary agreement which would grant to the parties concerned a further extension of time to arrive at a definite arrangement. The
federal authorities are of the opinion-and we respect their opinion without sharing it -that they have the right to impose taxes in one province to assist certain provincial projects in another province. The province of Quebec has always been and is still ready to co-operate reasonably and in a constitutional manner for the welfare and prosperity of the other provinces of the Canadian confederation.
It is beyond question that the revenue derived from taxes levied by Quebec, including the provincial tax on personal income, and which would be affected by the arrangements arrived at between Ottawa and the other provinces, it is beyond question, I say, that such revenue of the province of Quebec represents much smaller sums than the amount offered by Ottawa to the province of Quebec in its proposal to exchange important sources of provincial revenue for federal subsidies.
In short, the other provinces and the federal authorities, in our humble opinion, cannot reasonably object to the proposal we are making; first, because the amount collected by the province is financially less than the grant offered by the federal government and, secondly, because, as everyone agrees, the province is only exercising an indisputable right. It seems to us only elementary justice that the federal authorities should deduct from their tax on personal income paid to Ottawa by the taxpayers of Quebec, the amount of the provincial income tax which only after all represents a small fraction of the federal tax.
It is our profound conviction that the taxing powers which belong to the province of Quebec must be exercised by the province. These powers, which spring from dearly acquired rights and freedom, are indispensable to responsible government; they are also essential if the province is, freely and in accordance with its religious and national traditions, to exercise its rights and fulfil its obligations, amongst others, those pertaining to the vital fields of education and hospitalization.
In order to reach an agreement concerning the deduction of our provincial tax, we are ready to delete from our act authorizing a provincial tax on personal income the statements, in the preamble, to the effect that the province has a prior right in the matter of direct taxation.
Further, we shall give effect, by order in council, to the decision we have taken, a couple of months ago, with a view to making the tax payable to Quebec on undistributed income and dividends consistent with the federal act. In other words, by virtue of

such amendment, the province will only get 15 per cent of the rates authorized by the federal act in such cases.
Our provincial tax act on personal income is for a period of three years, that is to say, for each of the calendar years 1954, 1955 and 1956; we suggest that an agreement to be arrived at between Ottawa and Quebec should be for the same period.
The Quebec government wishes earnestly to reach an amicable settlement of this problem, and we express the hope that the above-mentioned provincial proposals will be favourably received by the federal authorities.
As I wrote you on October 11th, "if you decide to call a Canadian intergovernmental conference at Ottawa, we will be happy to attend and we will not hesitate to defer our parliamentary work should this conference take place during the session of our legislature".
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) M. L. DUPLESSIS

Ottawa, January 14, 1955
The Honourable Maurice L. Duplessis, Q.C., Premier of the Province of Quebec, Parliament Buildings,
Quebec, Que.
My dear Premier:
Since receiving your letter of November 1, my colleagues and I have considered at length the problem raised by the Quebec income tax and by the fact that the taxpayers having to pay it remain subject also to the federal tax.
This is, of course, an inevitable consequence of two jurisdictions exercising their concurrent rights to tax the incomes of the same persons. The only way you suggested to avoid the effect of double taxation upon the taxpayers of Quebec is for us to deduct from the federal tax on the income of each individual an amount equivalent to the amount which he is required to pay as the provincial tax.
In your letter, you state that the provincial tax "represents only approximately 10 per cent of the federal tax on personal income collected in the province of Quebec because, even though our provincial tax is apparently calculated to be 15 per cent of the federal tax, the exemptions provided by the provincial law materially reduce this proportion". In this quotation from your letter, you refer to two different aspects of the provincial law. When you state that the Quebec tax represents approximately 10 per cent of the federal tax you compare the yield of the provincial tax to the amount produced by the federal tax in the province of Quebec.
When you say that your tax "is apparently calculated to be 15 per cent of the federal tax", you explain this percentage by referring to the scale of exemptions granted by your law. This scale is such that it does not subject to your tax all the Quebec taxpayers who are obliged to pay the federal tax. In order to obtain an amount corresponding to 10 per cent of the amount yielded by the federal tax, it has been necessary to fix, for those who have to pay your tax, a higher rate than if you had distributed the burden oyer all those we tax.
Provincial legislatures have, like the federal parliament, the right and the responsibility to distribute the burden of their taxes on their taxpayers in whatever way seems most

appropriate to them. This is a right and a responsibility which is the same for all provinces, and none of them can be compelled to conform with the course of action followed elsewhere. Whatever differences there may be in the rules adopted by the different provinces, the federal law must be the same everywhere and it must be such as to leave the federal government with the revenues needed to fulfil its national responsibilities.
At present the federal law allows every Canadian taxpayer having to pay a provincial personal income tax to claim a deduction up to 5 per cent of his federal tax. This method of deduction raises certain administrative difficulties and, what is more serious, it makes the real incidence of the provincial tax depend on the terms of the federal law and makes the total amount deducted from the federal tax depend on the terms of the provincial law. Instead of deducting the provincial tax from the federal tax, we intend to propose to parliament a reduction of the federal tax for all taxpayers of a province having a provincial tax, whether or not they have to pay the provincial tax. Thus, the taxpayers of such a province will receive the benefit of the total amount of the reduction in the federal tax and the federal and provincial authorities will be able to determine, independently of one another, in what way and to what extent their taxpayers will be subjected to their respective taxes.
The 5 per cent deduction allowed at present by the federal law was fixed in 1946. Since that time, two changes have occurred. In the first place, the rates of the federal tax have been reduced with the result that there has been a corresponding reduction in the amount represented by the 5 per cent. In addition, the tax rentals paid by the federal government to the provinces under the tax agreements have been rising as a consequence of the increase in the population and in the national product.
Pending the results of a new federal-provincial conference, we propose therefore to ask parliament to amend the federal income tax law in order to grant a reduction of 10 per cent to all taxpayers of any province where a provincial income tax is levied whether or not all these taxpayers have to pay the provincial tax. We will recommend that this amendment apply to the years 1955 and 1956. At the same time, we will ask parliament to release from its present agreement any province which would prefer this new arrangement and I am immediately so informing the other premiers.
Moreover, we feel it would be reasonable to make the new percentage apply to taxpayers who have been in fact subjected to two

taxes on their 1954 income. We intend, therefore, to propose that the taxpayers who will have paid provincial income tax for 1954 be allowed a deduction up to 10 per cent of their federal tax.
We hope that this action on our part will encourage your government to act in the same spirit and that we will have, on both sides, helped to prepare the atmosphere for useful and fruitful work during the next federal-provincial conference.
In any event, we would have had to meet before the end of 1955 to discuss the fiscal relations of the years which will follow the expiry of the present tax rental agreements. We feel that it might be appropriate to begin the new conference at an earlier date, if that is possible. Upon my return from the commonwealth meeting in London, towards the middle of February, I intend to communicate with the premiers of all the provinces with a view to working out arrangements for a conference and fixing a date for it.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) LOUIS S. ST. LAURENT

My dear Premier:
You will no doubt have learned from the press that I have been in communication with the premier of Quebec about the situation created for personal income taxpayers in that province resulting from the imposition of a provincial income tax applicable in the years 1954, 1955 and 1956.
Before this provincial tax was imposed, the situation in Quebec was that the income taxpayers of that province were paying federal taxes at the same rate as other Canadians although the people of Quebec were not receiving the financial advantage for their provincial services that the people of the other provinces were receiving through the tax rental agreements.
Since the imposition of the provincial tax many of the personal income taxpayers in Quebec are required to pay higher personal income taxes than other Canadians, and payments under the tax rental agreements are still unavailable to the people of that province, because the government of the province preferred, as was its right, not to conclude an agreement.
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Relations
At the time the provincial tax was imposed, the provincial authorities suggested publicly that the total amount of the tax paid to the province should, be allowed by the federal authorities as a tax credit against the federal income tax.
If the federal government had accepted this suggestion, we would have felt obliged to make the same concession to any other province, and this would have meant that the effective rate of federal taxation in each province would have been set by the provincial authorities and would have differed from one province to another. We felt that the federal law must be uniform in its application in all provinces.
We did indicate, however, that the federal government was not wedded to the principle of tax rental agreements to the exclusion of any better alternative arrangement if one could be found. At the same time, we made it clear that the present government had no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements which is to make it financially possible for all the provinces, whatever their tax base, to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation. That is the foundation of the policy of the federal government.
I had a meeting with the premier of Quebec at his request in October and he indicated,# at that time, that he was considering making certain amendments to the provincial tax law which he hoped might make some temporary arrangement possible. My colleagues and I felt it was our duty to make every effort to find some alternative to the tax rental agreements which would preserve the fundamental objective of those agreements which I have mentioned and at the same time be more acceptable to all provincial governments.

This method of deduction raises certain administrative difficulties and, what is even more serious, it makes the real incidence of the provincial tax depend on the terms of the federal law and makes the. total amount deducted from the federal tax depend on the terms of the provincial law. Instead of deducting the provincial tax from the federal tax we intend to propose a reduction of the federal tax for all taxpayers of a province having a provincial tax, whether or not they have to pay the provincial tax. Thus, the taxpayers of such a province will receive the benefit of the total amount of the reduction in the federal tax and the federal and provincial authorities will be able to determine, independently of one another, in what way and to what extent their taxpayers will be subjected to their respective taxes.
The 5 per cent deduction allowed at present by the federal law was fixed in 1946. Since that time, two changes have occurred. In the first place, the rates of the federal tax have been reduced with the result that there has been a corresponding reduction in the amount represented by the 5 pef cent. In addition, the tax rentals paid by the federal government to the provinces under the tax agreements have been rising as a consequence of the increase in the population and in the national product.
Pending the results of a new federal-provincial conference, we propose, therefore, to ask parliament to amend the federal

income tax law in order to grant a reduction of 10 per cent to all taxpayers of any province where a provincial income tax is levied whether or not all these taxpayers have to pay the provincial tax. We will recommend that this amendment apply to the years 1955 and 1956. At the same time, we will ask parliament to release from its present agreement any province which would prefer this new arrangement.
Moreover, we feel it would be reasonable to make the new percentage apply to taxpayers who have been in fact subjected to two taxes on their 1954 income. We intend, therefore, to propose that income taxpayers who will have paid a provincial tax for 1954 be allowed a deduction up to 10 per cent of their federal tax.
I shall be glad to know at your convenience whether your government would wish to be released from the tax rental agreement in order to take advantage of the proposed new arrangement for 1955 and 1956.
It had always been understood that it would be necessary to hold a federal-provincial conference before the end of 1955 to discuss fiscal arrangements for the years which will follow the present tax rental agreements. In the light of recent developments it might be the desire of the provincial governments to have this conference held at an earlier date.
I shall accordingly communicate with you again shortly after my return from the commonwealth prime ministers' meeting in London towards the middle of February with a view to working out arrangements for a conference at a time which will be satisfactory to all governments concerned.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) LOUIS S. ST. LAURENT
Tuesday, January 18, 1955
